title: Design Space Exploration of Reinforcement Learning Configurations for Post-Legalization Placement
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) have recently been explored for VLSI placement optimization, but their effectiveness for post-legalization placement refinement remains unclear. This paper presents a systematic design space exploration of a GNN-Proximal Policy Optimization (GNN-PPO) framework across three ISPD2015 benchmarks. We evaluate 18 configurations covering reward functions, GNN architectures, action spaces, candidate-set sizes, and training strategies. We analyse the results we obtain to identify pitfalls and to assess the prospects and opportunities of the RL methods for post-legalization placement. On top of that we propose a design classification approach to guide the design decisions of RL models.

title: Beyond DFT electronic band structures via dual-space orbital learning
abstract: Accurate electronic band structures are essential for predicting material properties, but high-fidelity calculations are computationally demanding. We introduce O-kRystal, a dual-space orbital-learning framework that uses a lower-cost Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) calculation as both an energy baseline and a source of structured orbital information. Combining PBE band energies with real- and reciprocal-space orbital matrices, O-kRystal predicts higher-level corrections for individual electronic states as a function of crystal momentum and spin. For states within 5 eV of the band-edge midpoint, it predicts Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (HSE06) band energies with a mean absolute error of $0.171 \pm 0.009$ eV across nearly 6,000 three-dimensional materials spanning insulating, metallic, magnetic, and nonmagnetic systems. On a separate benchmark of six strongly correlated materials, it reduces the corresponding PBE band-energy MAE by 68.7% and resolves orbital-dependent changes in the relative placement of transition-metal d and ligand p states. Despite training only at high-symmetry points, it maintains comparable accuracy at unseen points along band paths and reconstructs HSE06 densities of states from dense Brillouin-zone predictions. Finally, training O-kRystal on $G_0W_0$ quasiparticle energies for two-dimensional materials demonstrates its applicability across levels of theory and the potential of orbital learning for higher-fidelity, momentum-resolved electronic-structure prediction beyond density functional theory.

title: Robota-Embed: Unified VLA Embeddings for Robot In-Context Learning and Evolution
abstract: Retrieving useful context for a robot requires matching its task, execution stage, and the continuation that should follow. We introduce Robota-Embed, to our knowledge the first vision-language-action (VLA) embedding model to jointly encode all three modalities in both current-state queries and recorded future continuations. Predictive retrieval training aligns these endpoints, enabling historical continuations to serve as context at inference time. We construct a multi-source corpus of 1,695,684 cleaned training anchors and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench, with 4,000 queries and a shared 8,000-entry gallery. Robota-Embed achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, exceeding action-free Gemini Embedding 2 by 22.09 and 33.47 percentage points. Controlled retrieval studies show that removing native action degrades retrieval more than removing vision. We study two complementary applications. Embed2ICL uses retrieved experience for training-free and training-based policy conditioning, increasing success from 47.0% to 56.3% in DROID-Sim and from 86.4% to 92.8% on the LIBERO difficult subset, while improving task progress on real robots. Embed2Evolve uses execution feedback to grow task-local memory and refine context use around a frozen GPT-6 Astra policy. Across five ManiSkill tasks, it achieves 68% success, compared with 24% for GPT-6 Astra Direct and 33% for a harness independently evolved with Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B under the same protocol. Relative to the latter, it uses approximately 79.5% fewer policy tokens per test rollout, counting both successes and failures. These results show that a unified, action-aware retrieval space can support robot in-context learning and task-local context evolution.

title: Smoothing out the edges: continuous-time estimation with Gaussian process motion priors on factor graphs
abstract: Continuous-time state estimation is gaining in popularity due to its abilities to provide smooth solutions, handle asynchronous sensors and interpolate between data points. While there are two main paradigms, parametric (e.g., temporal basis functions, splines) and nonparametric (Gaussian processes [GP]), the latter has seen less adoption despite its technical advantages and relative ease of implementation. This paper seeks to rectify this situation by providing a new simplified explanation of GP continuous-time estimation rooted in the language of factor graphs, which have become the de facto estimation paradigm in much of robotics. To simplify onboarding, this paper also provides three working examples implemented in the popular Georgia Tech Smoothing and Mapping estimation framework.

title: Dynamical Stability of an Operational Access Boundary Under Local Free Evolution
abstract: An earlier note derived, for two qubits coupled by a fixed controlled-NOT and an experimenterwith local capabilities on the target qubit only, that the accessible effects are exactly those of thealgebra A1 = M2 ⊗ span{I, Z}: a non-classical algebra is accessible while the control qubit’s phaseis not. That boundary was derived for a remainder with no dynamics of its own. This note askswhether it is maintained when the remainder evolves freely under a time-independent HamiltonianH = h1 X + h2 Y + h3 Z that is fixed and known, and the experimenter may insert waits ofany chosen duration, adaptively, anywhere in a protocol. The answer is an exact dichotomy. title: Verification package for "Verifying deployed bytecode against executable EVM semantics, with exact gas and no added axioms"
abstract: This package accompanies the paper "Verifying deployed bytecode against executable EVM semantics, with exact gas and no added axioms" (Seulkee Baek, 2026). It holds the records behind the paper's figures and tables, and the scripts that recompute them offline. The paper's statements refer to the Lean libraries Blanc, at commit 5048a51fb108d8d71dd58c897c4c62c8bff3b437 (archived by Software Heritage as swh:1:rev:5048a51fb108d8d71dd58c897c4c62c8bff3b437), and Jaune, at 2737c8ebcaec2f3a9a7014156403300bc664daab (swh:1:rev:2737c8ebcaec2f3a9a7014156403300bc664daab), with Lean v4.34.0. The proofs themselves live in those repositories; this package does not duplicate them. What it contains:- the on-chain records read for the paper at block 26,141,229 (7 October 2026) from three public RPC providers, including every WETH9 withdrawal and Uniswap V2 approve receipt compared in Sections 2.4 and 5.1 and Appendices C and D, the block-isolation records, the scripts that read them, and their outputs;- the commit-bound figures of the paper (library metrics, the generated-code share, the cost table, the claim map), each with the command that produced it, and `final-5048a51f/figures.md`, which maps every figure in the paper to its source;- the conformance-case inventory of the fixture release tests@v20.0.2;- `reproduce.py`, an offline entry point that, given clones of Blanc and Jaune, recomputes the commit-bound figures and the receipt comparisons from the shipped inputs and checks them against the recorded results; it needs Python 3.11 or newer and Git, no Python packages, no Lean and no network access. How to run it: git clone https://github.com/skbaek/blanc && git clone https://github.com/skbaek/jaunepython3 -I verification-package/reproduce.py --blanc blanc --jaune jaune \ --data verification-package --out NEW_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY The output directory must not exist. On success the run prints one OK line, preceded by two SKIPPED lines for the third-party comparisons described below; any mismatch stops it with an error. The proofs are checked by building Blanc at the commit above (see the paper's Appendix E and Blanc's scripts/GATES.md), not by this script. What was left out, and why: copies of third-party documents (audit reports, papers, saved web pages, verified source files of others' contracts and the Uniswap npm build artifacts) are not redistributed here. THIRD_PARTY.md and third_party.json list each one with its original location and SHA-256, so a reader can fetch it and check it is the same file. Two of them, the @uniswap/v2-core build artifacts, feed two comparisons of reproduce.py (the npm factory runtime against the chain's bytes, and the npm pair runtime against the lifted bytes); without them the script reports those two comparisons as SKIPPED, and with them in place it runs them in full (`--require-third-party` makes their absence an error). The author's internal review notes and drafting history are also left out. Licences: scripts (.py, .sh, .swift) are under the MIT licence (LICENSE-MIT); all other files are under CC BY 4.0 (LICENSE-CC-BY-4.0), except ext/verity-ci-axiom-report-d42019149188/, a copy of Verity's own CI axiom report, which remains under Verity's MIT licence (see its PROVENANCE.md), and onchain/eips/eip-7002.txt and eip-7600.txt, text renderings of those EIPs, whose copyright is waived via CC0.

title: Learning-enabled collaborative intelligence in search and rescue robotics: a survey of paradigms, models, and challenges
abstract: Search and Rescue (SAR) robotics increasingly depends on collaborative intelligence to operate effectively in dynamic, uncertain, and time-sensitive environments. Modern SAR missions require coordinated interaction among heterogeneous robotic agents as well as structured collaboration between humans and intelligent systems for perception, decision-making, and adaptive mission execution. This paper presents a structured narrative review supported by a systematic literature search of learning-enabled collaborative intelligence frameworks in SAR robotics, organized around three paradigms: human-to-machine (H2M), machine-to-machine (M2M), and machine-to-human (M2H) learning. The review examines recent developments in reinforcement learning, federated and decentralized learning, knowledge distillation, swarm intelligence, semantic communication, and the growing integration of large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) for knowledge grounding, transfer, and explainability. Beyond algorithmic advances, the analysis emphasizes deployment-oriented challenges including partial observability, communication constraints, uncertainty management, model reliability, and real-time operational requirements. Rather than conducting a fully PRISMA-compliant systematic review, this work synthesizes representative and influential studies to identify emerging trends, architectural trade-offs, deployment limitations, and future research directions for scalable and trustworthy collaborative SAR systems.

title: Semantic Wave Function Collapse: Natural-Language-Guided Constrained World Generation
abstract: Natural-language instructions can describe scenes through mandatory requirements, preferences, and contextual information. Conventional Wave Function Collapse (WFC) enforces local pattern compatibility but cannot, by itself, interpret these instructions or guarantee global requirements such as object counts and connectivity. We introduce Semantic-Constrained Probabilistic WFC (SC-PWFC), a compiler-generator-verifier framework that translates language into typed, executable scene specifications. SC-PWFC combines hard constraints, soft preferences, and contextual priors in an explicit probabilistic model. During scene construction, WFC-style propagation enforces local compatibility, global feasibility checks reject impossible partial scenes, and an independent verifier checks completed scenes. The framework also supports constrained completion, localized editing, and explicit handling of ambiguity and infeasibility. Controlled experiments demonstrate more accurate semantic compilation, more efficient constraint-aware generation, improved preference satisfaction and contextual consistency, and reliable preservation of protected content during editing. SC-PWFC thus extends WFC beyond local pattern generation towards language-guided, probabilistic, and verifiable scene synthesis.

title: From Detection to Decision: Calibration and Deferral for Prompt-Injection Detection
abstract: Prompt-injection defenses are commonly evaluated as binary detectors, although deployed LLM applications must make operational decisions about whether to allow, block, or escalate potentially malicious inputs. Recent probabilistic decision models aim to support such decisions through calibrated confidence estimates, but their reliability under distribution shift remains uncertain. We evaluate a native probabilistic decision model (Jev), two Llama Prompt Guard 2 classifiers (22M and 86M), and an LLM-based judge on 47,611 held-out examples spanning direct and indirect prompt injections, hard-benign inputs, obfuscation, and distribution shift. Using separate development and calibration splits, we assess detection performance, probability calibration, and allow-block-defer policies under a frozen evaluation protocol. The LLM judge achieves the highest overall discrimination (AUROC 0.897), followed by Jev (0.871), Prompt Guard 2 86M (0.757), and Prompt Guard 2 22M (0.714). However, Jev's native probabilities do not consistently outperform post-hoc calibrated classifier scores, and temperature scaling improves calibration without improving discrimination. At an empirical false-negative-rate target of 1%, all evaluated gate-reviewer systems require more than 91.8% escalation and incur substantial false-positive rates. These findings demonstrate that probabilistic outputs alone do not establish reliable security decisions under distribution shift. Effective LLM security systems must jointly evaluate detection, calibration, reviewer behavior, and operational decision policies.

title: SHRED: Self-Play for Heterogeneous Road-Users without Expert Demonstrations
abstract: Realistic traffic simulation and autonomous planning both depend on modeling interactions among heterogeneous road users whose dynamics, constraints, and behaviors differ fundamentally. Existing approaches predominantly learn realistic interaction behavior from large-scale human driving demonstrations. In this work, we ask whether such behavior can instead emerge purely through self-play. We present SHRED, a framework that jointly trains vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists through large-scale heterogeneous self-play from random initialization, without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay. SHRED combines type-specific dynamics and objectives with procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization, allowing diverse behaviors to emerge through closed-loop interaction. On the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC), SHRED jointly controls all three road-user types and outperforms both the closest demonstration-free self-play baseline and prior self-play methods that use demonstration-trained reference policies. Policies trained only on nuPlan map geometry retain comparable realism under zero-shot evaluation on Waymo. For planning, SHRED outperforms all compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark. Controlled ablations show that heterogeneity in self-play improves both traffic realism and planning performance, with particularly large planning gains in interaction-heavy scenarios. Together, these results establish heterogeneous procedural self-play as a scalable, demonstration-free paradigm for learning realistic and interactive traffic behavior.

title: Evaluating Model Capabilities After Benchmark Saturation
abstract: Rapid advances in AI capabilities are causing benchmarks to saturate. Once several models approach perfect scores, a benchmark loses its power to differentiate between them, and with it its utility for informing AI safety cases and frontier policies. Yet benchmark items produce far more information than the scores we typically extract from them: a full transcript of how each model solved the task. We investigate whether these transcripts can be used to assess model capabilities even after benchmark scores have saturated. We simulate saturation retrospectively using historical benchmark and model releases, and test whether protocols that access only correctly solved transcripts from saturated benchmarks can predict capabilities measured on held-out, unsaturated items. We evaluate representative contemporary approaches for extracting information from model transcripts: pairwise judging, single-transcript absolute scoring, and predictions from deterministic transcript features or embeddings. We find that saturated transcripts retain capability information beyond benchmark accuracy. Amongst our evaluated protocols, pairwise judging performs best, reducing prediction error by 5.3 times compared to a baseline using only saturated benchmark scores. This capability-relevant information is distributed across transcript sections, but concentrated in specific channels of information such as reasoning and tool-calls. However, the predictive power of protocols does not always generalise across distribution shifts -- for example by underestimating the capabilities of the first reasoning models introduced in early 2025. Saturated benchmarks thus retain capability-predicting signal in their task transcripts, but extending the lifetime of existing benchmarks requires methods designed to extract these signals robustly.

title: AdaRSI: On-Demand Recursive Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) often fail midway through unseen long-horizon tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a remedy, but embodied RSI methods either refine the harness around a frozen executor and so cannot add a missing motion, or train the executor on persistent failures without asking whether a failure lies in how the executor is called or in what it can do. We ask when a self-improving embodied system should change the weights of its executor, and propose AdaRSI, an on-demand RSI framework for embodied agents. A coding agent first improves its skills and harness, then attributes persistent failures by retrying failing sub-steps from saved states, and fine-tunes only the sub-steps that remain unreliable, with demonstrations it collects itself and experience carried over from earlier tasks. On all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, with GR00T N1.5 as the executor and no human demonstrations, AdaRSI improves the VLA on all three suites and raises its success on unseen composite tasks from 4.6% to 13.8%. Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, it reaches slightly higher success while using only 28% of the GPU time and 22% of the self-collected demonstrations, and fine-tuning without a harness trains more yet gains far less.

title: Uncertainty-Driven Self-Play for Robust Multi-Agent Driving Policies
abstract: Learning robust driving policies that generalize beyond their training domain remains a central challenge in motion planning. We propose an uncertainty-driven self-play scheme, in which half of the agents are rewarded for increasing their neighbors' epistemic uncertainty, while the other half learn to drive safely as the exploring agents continuously seek out their weaknesses. Epistemic uncertainty indicates where the policy is least confident and serves as an automatic proxy for scenario difficulty. Exploring agents use this signal to seek out hard cases, generating a challenging curriculum without manual scenario design. The resulting policy outperforms standard self-play, achieving best-in-class zero-shot transfer to nuplan Val14 (99.12% vs. 97.97%) and Argoverse 2 (82.39% vs. 78.03%) without fine-tuning, while also improving performance over standard self-play on Waymo. Our diversity-driven approach achieves 85% higher LSTM hidden-state coverage than the baseline, indicating a much richer set of behaviors. Further analysis shows that epistemic uncertainty serves as a calibrated difficulty detector, with highest-uncertain agents exhibiting 14.8 times the combined failure rate across collision, off-road, and DNF, of lowest-uncertain agents, enabling automatic prioritization of challenging scenarios without ground-truth labels.

title: Shot- and Noise-Aware Pauli Correlation Encoding for Max-Cut Experiments on IBM Heron Quantum Processor
abstract: Pauli correlation encoding (PCE) encodes $m$ binary variables in the signs of $k$-body Pauli correlators of $n=O(m^{1/k})$ qubits, and trains a parameterized circuit on a relaxed loss of sharpness $α$. The strongest published schedules sharpen this loss aggressively and are benchmarked with exact expectation values, whereas a quantum computer estimates correlators from a finite number of shots. We show that the sharpness is a hidden shot budget. Since the expected sign of a correlator estimated from $S$ shots, $\mathrm{erf}(c\sqrt{S/2})$, agrees with $\tanh(0.851\sqrt{S}\,c)$ to within $0.019$, the edge term of the relaxed loss at $α=0.851\sqrt{S}$ approximately equals, up to a constant, minus twice the cut expected from decoding $S$ shots. This explains why schedules tuned with exact expectation values lose their advantage at realistic budgets, and yields a shot-aware schedule whose final sharpness is set by the shot budget. On five G-set graphs with $800$ variables on $13$ qubits, this schedule outperforms every published schedule at its target budget in all $150$ paired comparisons of the decoded circuit output, owing to the sharpness at $1.6\times10^4$ shots and mostly to switching off the regularization at $10^3$; after a classical bit-swap search, it remains the best on average at $1.6\times10^4$ shots. Device noise damps the correlators by a factor $s$, which amounts to a smaller shot budget $s^2S$. On the IBM Heron processor ibm_fez, an all-to-all ansatz of the type used for the best published G-set results compiles to $835$ CZ gates and decodes to a random cut, while our $96$-CZ hardware-native circuit, trained in simulation and sharpened to $α\simeq0.65\,s\sqrt{S}$, retains up to $0.919$ of the best-known cut. For new circuits, a damping and an offset calibrated on other circuits of the same graph predicted the decoded cuts at $10^3$ shots to within $0.002$.

On the IBM Heron processor ibm_fez, an all-to-all ansatz of the type used for the best published G-set results compiles to $835$ CZ gates and decodes to a random cut, while our $96$-CZ hardware-native circuit, trained in simulation and sharpened to $α\simeq0.65\,s\sqrt{S}$, retains up to $0.919$ of the best-known cut. title: Robust Real-Time Monocular Human Pose Estimation with Insole-Based Sensor Fusion
abstract: Real-time monocular human pose estimation is an important sensing component for human-centered intelligent systems. While recent camera-based methods have achieved impressive accuracy, fundamental challenges persist, particularly when visual observations are incomplete, such as during lower-body occlusion or short out-of-frame intervals. In these challenging but common scenarios, vision-only systems often struggle to reconstruct physically plausible lower-limb motion and reliable foot-ground contact. Due to the highly unobtrusive and wearable nature of smart insoles, this paper investigates whether simple plantar pressure and acceleration sensors can effectively resolve these visually induced limitations. To systematically investigate this, we first collect a synchronized multimodal dataset and then propose a part-decoupled temporal fusion framework. The proposed model fuses foot-sensing features into the lower-body branch to compensate for incomplete visual evidence, while a lightweight coordinator exchanges information between the upper- and lower-body temporal representations to maintain whole-body consistency. The framework is evaluated with three representative real-time visual backbones based on 2D keypoints, 3D landmarks, and SMPL-based human mesh recovery. We evaluate our framework on three representative real-time visual backbones. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that incorporating simple foot sensors consistently improves pose accuracy, motion smoothness, and gait-related measurements over vision-only baselines, with the most significant gains observed under occlusion and short visual-dropout conditions. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that unobtrusive foot sensing provides vital and complementary physical observability when camera observations are temporarily unavailable.

title: Sequence models reveal diagnosis accumulation pathways beyond comorbidity burden in population-scale hospital data
abstract: Aging trajectories vary among individuals of similar age and disease burden. Comorbidity indices, e.g. the Elixhauser index, aggregate recorded conditions into a single score, but discard the timing, sequence, and pace of morbidity accumulation. Here we ask whether longitudinal hospital diagnosis histories contain information beyond age, sex, and comorbidity burden, and where it is concentrated. Using 13 years of Austrian inpatient data covering 7.4 million patients, we trained a visit-level contrastive transformer to encode diagnosis sequences and inter-admission timing into patient-history embeddings. In a downstream cohort of 1.7 million individuals, the embedding model improved prediction of in-hospital death over the Elixhauser-based comorbidity model, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.879 versus 0.866 (AUC gain = 0.0132, 95% CI 0.0118–0.0144). Across 130 incident ICD-10 disease-block outcomes, the embedding model had higher AUC for 93 outcomes, with a modest median gain of 0.006. Gains were concentrated in mental, musculoskeletal, nervous system, and metabolic disorders. We then evaluated event-free survival, defined as remaining alive without accumulating a second unrecorded ICD-10 disease block. The embedding model achieved an AUC of 0.726 versus 0.722 for the comorbidity model. However, among patients with similar age, sex, and comorbidity-model risk, those assigned high residual risk had 127–181 fewer event-free days over five years and observed event rates comparable to low-residual-risk patients more than a decade older. Together, these findings link the embedding’s signal to the breadth, recency, and pace of prior disease accumulation.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Learning and Collaborative Learning for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can improve their task performance through individual self-improvement mechanisms, while multi-agent LLM systems can leverage communication, feedback, and coordination to solve problems that exceed the capabilities of individual agents. However, independently learning and collaboratively learning are often implemented as separate mechanisms or combined through predefined workflows. A system that always learns independently may fail to exploit complementary knowledge across models, whereas a system that always collaborates may incur unnecessary communication costs, propagate incorrect information, and reduce the benefits of independent exploration. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching between Self-Learning and Collaborative Learning for Multiple Large Language Models (ASCL-LLM), a conceptual framework in which multiple LLM agents dynamically switch between independent self-learning and collaborative learning according to task difficulty, uncertainty, learning progress, disagreement, estimated improvement, communication costs, and historical outcomes. Each agent maintains an individual learning state while participating in a shared collaborative process when appropriate. A meta-controller selects the learning mode for each task or learning episode and updates its switching policy according to observed outcomes. The framework distinguishes task-level adaptation, episode-level adaptation, and longer-term adaptation of the switching policy. It also incorporates safeguards against negative knowledge transfer, redundant communication, and unstable self-reinforcement. The proposed framework is formalized as a sequential decision-making problem with two primary learning modes and an optional abstention or escalation mechanism for cases in which neither mode provides sufficient confidence. A cost-sensitive switching objective is developed to balance task performance, learning progress, computational expenditure, communication overhead, and reliability. A comprehensive experimental protocol is proposed to compare adaptive switching with self-learning-only, collaborative-learning-only, fixed-schedule, random-switching, and confidence-based baselines. The framework provides a testable research direction for constructing multi-LLM systems that can determine not only how to learn, but also when to learn independently and when to learn collaboratively. Its effectiveness remains an empirical question requiring implementation and evaluation.

title: An Efficient AES-128 CMOS Architecture with Round Reuse and Composite Field S-Box to Secure IoT Devices
abstract: The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has intensified the demand for lightweight cryptographic solutions that deliver high security without compromising energy and area constraints. This paper presents a highly efficient AES -128 hardware architecture specifically optimised for resource-constrained IoT devices. The proposed design employs reusing a 128 -bit AES framework resource, enabling an extensive reduction in functional units across all transformation stages. Additionally, the elimination of intermediate registers and the reuse of a single round computation block for all encryption rounds significantly reduce area while balancing the trade -offs between throughput, frequency and power. A key innovation in this work is the implementation of a compact S-box using composite Galois Field GF28 arithmetic to enhance the substitution efficiency while maintaining cryptographic strength. The physical layout implemented on 32 nm technology reveals that the proposed architecture achieves a core area of only 0.015 mm , an operating 2 frequency of 200 MHz, with 0.014 Gbps throughput, and a low power consumption of 1.4 mW , offering a well-balanced trade-off among performance, security, and hardware efficiency. A comparative analysis with state-of-the-art designs demonstrates the superiority of this approach for achieving low-cost, energy-aware cryptographic protection. The proposed solution is highly suitable for secure resource constrained IoT deployments.

title: Trustworthy LLM Harnesses: A Measurement Framework for Correctness, Quality, Efficiency, Reliability, Robustness, Safety, and Fairness
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are no longer deployed as bare models. They run inside an execution harness, the control layer that assembles context, exposes tools, manages memory and state, schedules retries, and verifies intermediate results. Because the harness determines what the model sees and what its outputs are allowed to do, observed agent behavior is jointly produced by the model and the harness, yet prevailing benchmarks attribute it to the model alone. We study the problem of harness evaluation: holding the model, task distribution, environment, budget, and evaluator fixed, how can the contribution of the harness be isolated, and what does it mean for a harness to be trustworthy? We formalize the harness as a trajectory-generating policy and define the harness effect as a paired, metric-indexed contrast. We then develop measurement principles along seven dimensions—outcome correctness, quality, efficiency, reliability and reproducibility, robustness, safety, and fairness—each targeting the specific mechanisms through which a harness influences agent behavior, and grounded in established results from statistical evaluation, efficient inference, certified robustness, and fair learning. A set of elementary propositions clarifies when paired designs reduce variance, how approximate verification bounds correctness loss, why marginal subgroup gaps can mislead, and how differential evaluator bias contaminates harness comparisons. We conclude with a reference protocol and argue that harness quality should be reported as a Pareto profile rather than a single leaderboard score.

title: Introduction to GPT-5 (OpenAI)
abstract: This chapter provides an executive summary of GPT-5 as OpenAI’s 2025 flagship multimodal LLM, highlighting its focus on multi-step reasoning, large-context synthesis, software-engineering workflows (via GPT-5-Codex-Spark), adjustable thinking time, reliable tool use, and improved safety behaviors. It then compares GPT-5 with other leading models (GPT-4o/o3/o4, Claude 3.7, Gemini 2.x, Llama 3.x, DeepSeek) and briefly introduces the newly released GPT-5.4 and OpenAI Symphony multi-agent orchestration framework. This chapter emphasizes GPT-5’s quality-of-life improvements and positions it as a strong general-purpose model with specialized variants for coding and agentic tasks. This chapter then demonstrates GPT-5’s ability to generate Python/Matplotlib code for business-oriented and artistic visualizations. It includes examples of bar charts with alternating black/gray colors, bar charts with smooth black/gray gradient fills, labeled bar charts, and randomly generated circles. Each code listing is accompanied by a step-by-step explanation and a placeholder for the resulting figure. The examples show how GPT-5 can produce visually appealing, labeled, and gradient-filled charts with minimal prompting. The final section of this chapter explores GPT-5’s capacity to create more advanced artistic graphics using polar equations in Python/Matplotlib. It explains that no prior knowledge of polar equations is required, as the model generates complete, runnable code for visually interesting patterns. This chapter concludes by noting that some concepts (schemas, cosine similarity) are not explained in detail here and directs readers to external resources for deeper understanding. Overall, this chapter showcases GPT-5’s strength in producing both practical business graphics and esthetically pleasing mathematical art with clear code commentary. Please keep in mind that some of the code samples in this chapter involve concepts that are not explained in this chapter, such as schemas and cosine similarity. However, you can avail yourself of many free online articles that describe their purpose.

title: On the Stability and Convergence of Flow Map Training
abstract: Flow maps are a recent method of probabilistic generation that amortize diffusion trajectories into one-step samplers, unlocking efficient generation. While progress has been made in improving their empirical performance, there is still a lack of understanding behind the mechanisms underlying their success. Specifically, many flow map learning methods employ stop gradient operators as a crucial part of their training target. Adaptive weighting also drastically improves the generation capabilities of flow maps. Although many interpretations have been proposed to support the inclusion of these heuristics, none have analyzed the impact of these assumptions on the training dynamics of flow maps themselves. In this work, we address this issue by providing grounded theory explaining why such tricks are required. Analyzing the functional gradient flow induced by the MeanFlow and Lagrangian losses, we show their convergence to the true flow map, settling the validity of these objectives. For finite updates, we highlight a severe roadblock to the usage of these losses in practice: the possible unboundedness of the update. Adaptive normalization not only provides bounded updates, but, combined with a specific weighting, additionally provides convergence guarantees towards a neighborhood of the solution. On synthetic data, we show that our functional gradient flow analysis exactly describes the true training dynamics for flow maps. Experiments on standard image datasets demonstrate that a proper reweighting scheme is essential for strong empirical performance, which is only achieved for a specific range of reweighting strengths.

title: Equiangular weighted frames and conical 2-designs with unequal traces
abstract: Abstract Conical 2-designs are families of positive operators possessing crucial symmetry properties that allow them to eciently characterize important quantum measures. However, little is known about their general structures and properties. We propose a construction method of conical 2-designs whose elements are not of equal traces, based on a generalization of equiangular weighted frames to non-projective operators. We provide a detailed analysis of their properties, relations to quantum measurements, and applications, together with examples that go beyond the known classes. This constitutes a major step toward a full characterization of informationally overcomplete quantum measurements.

title: Bypassing the Kantian Limit: A First-Principles Rebuttal to DeepMind's Abductive Bottleneck via Cyber-Physical Homeostatic Regulation and Negative Constraint Vectors
abstract: The trajectory of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) has recently intersected with a profound theoretical and epistemological bottleneck. Recent scholarship from Google DeepMind posits that current artificial intelligence paradigms, specifically Large Language Models (LLMs), are structurally incapable of profound scientific invention because they lack the capacity for "abductive leaps". According to this critique, generative AI excels at inductive pattern matching and deductive logic but fails to generate novel explanatory hypotheses because it remains trapped in a disembodied digital vacuum, entirely reliant on pre-existing symbolic data. This white paper serves as a direct, first-principles rebuttal to that conclusion. The limitation identified by DeepMind is not an intrinsic boundary of artificial intelligence, but rather a localized artifact of relying on probabilistic pattern-matching algorithms devoid of sensory grounding and deterministic mathematical physics constructs. By replacing statistical token-prediction models with a Cyber-Physical Homeostatic Regulation Architecture, artificial intelligence can achieve true abductive reasoning and epistemological sovereignty. This paradigm shift, pioneered through the intellectual property and frameworks of Lifeline AI by founder and CEO/CTO Syed Abraham Ahmed, leverages Negative Constraint Vectors (NCVs), the Meta-Cognitive Governance Core (MGC), Deep-Relationship Dynamic Bayesian Neural-Networks with Time-Varying Neural Parameters (DR-DBNN-TPNV), molecular dynamic machine learning contracts, and hardware-tethered deterministic physics. By decoupling generative engines from validation engines, the architecture allows the AI to learn in first principles directly from physical, real-world thermodynamic failures. These physical failures are brought back into the generative engine to geometrically mutate the latent space, allowing the system to genuinely fail forward. Through the application of Bipartite Dynamic Slicing, Adjoint Backward Passes, Non-Intrusive Least Squares Shadowing (NILSS), and isometric Tensor Network States (isoTNS), the architecture bypasses the combinatorial explosion of chaotic systems. This paper rigorously details how anchoring causal discovery in absolute thermodynamic nullity and executing hardware-tethered geometric repulsion allows AI to shatter the Kantian Limit, achieving omni-deterministic scientific discovery and establishing the definitive blueprint for true AGI. Furthermore, While the core Cyber-physical Homeostatic Regulation Architecture, the Meta-Cognitive Governance Core (MGC), underlying Negative Constraint Vectors (NCV) architectures and molecular dynamic machine learning contracts, and hardware-tethered deterministic physics are governed by proprietary and patent-pending frameworks, scheduled to be published globally in November, 2026, comprehensive supporting validation materials are available. These include the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), and the (International Search Authority) (ISA) Written report, citing zero prior art teaching the technology and formally confirms the architecture’s strict fulfillment of all patentability requirements, including Novelty (N), Inventive Step (IS), and Industrial Applicability (IA).

title: Adaptive Reasoning and Collaborative Reasoning Switching Across Parallel Worlds of Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can improve complex problem-solving through deliberate reasoning, multiple reasoning trajectories, self-evaluation, and collaboration among agents. However, existing approaches often emphasize one dominant reasoning configuration, such as independent reasoning, parallel sampling, iterative self-refinement, or multi-agent collaboration. These configurations may be inefficient when task difficulty, uncertainty, reasoning progress, and computational constraints vary dynamically. This paper proposes Adaptive Parallel-World Reasoning and Collaboration (APW-RC), a conceptual framework in which multiple reasoning worlds are instantiated from the same underlying LLM or from heterogeneous LLMs. Each parallel world explores a distinct reasoning direction and independently adapts its reasoning strategy according to local evidence, uncertainty, progress, and resource constraints. A coordination controller dynamically determines whether a world should continue independent adaptive reasoning, collaborate with other worlds, or request assistance from external models. Collaboration can occur between worlds instantiated from the same model, between heterogeneous models, or across both groups. The framework combines trajectory diversity, local adaptation, selective information exchange, cross-model assistance, and cost-aware switching within a unified inference-time architecture. We formulate the switching problem as sequential decision-making under computational constraints and introduce a proposed objective that balances solution quality, reliability, diversity, latency, and computational expenditure. We also describe an implementation procedure, evaluation protocol, baseline systems, ablation studies, and potential failure modes. The framework is a research proposal rather than an experimentally validated system. Its principal research question is whether adaptive switching between independent reasoning and collaborative reasoning across parallel worlds can improve the quality–cost trade-off compared with fixed-mode reasoning and conventional multi-agent collaboration.

title: Prediction of Concrete Compressive Strength Using Ensemble Machine Learning Models Optimized by Lyrebird Optimization Algorithm and Human Evolutionary Optimization Algorithm
abstract: Precise prediction of concrete compressive strength plays a crucial role in designing concrete mixtures and assessing their quality. In this study, optimized ensemble machine learning models are developed and evaluated based on the UCI Concrete Compressive Strength dataset that are collected from laboratory tests on concrete mixtures. The predictor variables include cement, blast furnace slag, fly ash, water, superplasticizer, coarse aggregate, fine aggregate, and curing age, while the response variable denotes the concrete compressive strength. Two ensemble regressors, namely the extra trees regressor (ETR) and extreme gradient boosting regressor (XGBR), are optimized with the Lyrebird optimization algorithm (LOA) and the human evolutionary optimization algorithm (HEOA). The particle swarm optimization (PSO) and genetic algorithm are considered as comparison metaheuristics. A repeated holdout validation scheme is adopted, dividing the dataset into training, validation, and test sets at a ratio of 70:15:15. The validation set is used for selecting hyperparameters guided by the optimizer, while the test set is exclusively used to evaluate the final performance of the model. The nested cross-validation approach is not applied to optimize our proposed models. In this study, optimized XGBR-based models show better predictive performance than the ETR-based models. In particular, XGBR + PSO performed the best, with an R 2 value of 0.9486 ± 0.0182 and an RMSE of 3.7756 ± 0.6602 MPa. Among the LOA- and HEOA-based models, XGBR+HEOA obtained the best performance, with an R 2 value of 0.9483 ± 0.0174 and an RMSE of 3.7928 ± 0.6860 MPa.

title: SNOAR: Self-training with Noise filtering, Observation adding, and Remixing for Speech Denoising Without Clean References
abstract: Unsupervised speech denoising methods such as MixIT and noisy-target training can be trained directly on noisy recordings, avoiding the sim-to-real gap of synthetic training data, but remain well below supervised performance. Teacher--student self-training, as in RemixIT, narrows this gap by remixing a teacher's estimates into new mixtures that supervise a student; however, since the student is trained only toward the teacher's estimates, teacher errors, in particular over-suppressed speech, are never recovered and propagate as the teacher is updated from the student. We propose SNOAR, a self-training framework that corrects the teacher's estimates before use: the noise leaked into its speech estimate is removed by differential noise filtering (DNF), and part of the noisy observation is added back in to restore suppressed speech and attenuate artifacts. We show that the two corrections depend on each other, as without DNF the loop collapses to the identity mapping. Compared to RemixIT, SNOAR is more stable along training and outperforms it in signal-based, perceptual, and word error rate metrics, reaching 97\% of the SI-SDR improvement of a fully-supervised topline on WHAM!; on real CHiME-3 recordings, it improves every metric of three different teachers, while RemixIT degrades their perceptual quality.

title: ChronoCulture: Evaluating Cultural Awareness Across Time in Large Language Models
abstract: Cultural attitudes and social norms evolve over time, yet most cultural benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) treat culture as a static attribute of a country or region. We introduce ChronoCulture, a benchmark of 10,360 temporal pairs built from longitudinal survey data across 72 countries. Each pair contains the same survey question asked in the same country in an older and a newer year, with full population response distributions as ground truth. Across six LLMs, we find that models can often predict a country's attitudes at one point in time but do not reliably capture how those attitudes change. Their predictions for different years tend to stay close together, failing to capture much of the observed change. Specifying the intended year in the prompt also offers little overall improvement in alignment with survey responses. These findings suggest that models often present a largely static picture of cultural attitudes, highlighting the need to evaluate cultural awareness across time.

title: MUCO: A Mani-Unit-Structured Manipulation Framework for Compositional Long-Horizon Robot Tasks
abstract: Learning and executing long-horizon robot manipulation as complete task trajectories raises data-collection costs, lim?its capability reuse, and causes local failures to cascade into later task stages. We introduce manipulation units (MUs) as reusable operations, each defined by a local goal, an initi?ation condition, and observable success and failure criteria. MUs are learned and verified individually. During execution, consecutive MUs remain coupled through shared environ?ment dynamics. We formulate MU-Structured Manipulation (MUSM) and realize it through MU-Centric Orchestration (MUCO). Given language and vision, MUCO constructs an MU sequence, matches each MU to compatible policy models in a frozen capability registry, and dispatches the model with the highest calibrated success rate. Visual verification checks MU outcomes against success and failure criteria and governs transitions, enabling retry or fallback to another model from the current state without re-executing verified MUs. Canonical keys enable checkpoint reuse for equivalent MUs across tasks without new demonstrations or updates. We evaluate MUCO on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks. MUCO achieves higher complete-task success and verified progress, stronger failure containment, and lower error propagation than baselines. Results demonstrate cross-task MU reuse and het?erogeneous policy composition without joint training, shared backbones, or common action representations.

title: Digital Self-Interference Cancellation for In-Band Full-Duplex Systems Based on Transformer Neural Operators
abstract: Digital-domain self-interference cancellation is essential in in-band full-duplex radios after passive suppression and analog cancellation. It is particularly challenging when the desired signal is strong relative to the residual self-interference. In this regime, conventional iterative digital cancellers update their coefficients from desired-signal-contaminated received samples and may suffer substantial performance degradation. This paper reformulates digital-domain self-interference cancellation as an operator-learning problem. The proposed framework learns the temporal evolution of the residual self-interference channel from historical observations and uses the learned operator together with the known local transmit signal to reconstruct the current residual self-interference. A Transformer neural operator is used to realize this framework. The resulting method is trained in a desired-signal-free setting and then applied in the presence of a desired signal. A continuity-based analysis characterizes the sensitivity of the learned operator to the resulting input perturbation. Numerical experiments in static and time-varying channels, including time-varying SIR conditions, demonstrate stable cancellation performance over a wide range of interference levels. At 30 dB SIR, the proposed method improves the cancellation performance by 5--15 dB over the considered conventional methods.

title: (2, m)-threshold quantum data hiding
abstract: Abstract Quantum data hiding aims to encode classical information into quantum states so that it can be recovered through suitable joint measurements while remaining inaccessible under local operations and classical communication (LOCC). Motivated by the question of whether quantum data hiding can be extended to a multiparty setting in which any pair of parties can recover the hidden information while it remains nearly inaccessible under LOCC, we investigate multiparty quantum state discrimination and propose a multiparty quantum data-hiding scheme for one classical bit shared among multiple parties. In the proposed scheme, any pair of parties can perfectly recover the hidden bit through a joint measurement, whereas LOCC measurements performed even by all parties can reveal only an arbitrarily small amount of information. We further derive bounds on the optimal LOCC discrimination of multiparty quantum states. The proposed scheme can be implemented using only separable states of low-dimensional quantum systems, thereby enhancing its practical feasibility.

title: INTELIGENCIA ARTIFICIAL PARA LA CARACTERIZACIÓN DE MASAS MAMARIAS BENIGNAS Y MALIGNAS MEDIANTE MAMOGRAFÍA Y ECOGRAFÍA
abstract: El cáncer de mama es la neoplasia maligna más frecuente en mujeres a nivel mundial, con aproximadamente 2,3 millones de casos nuevos anuales. La capacidad para diferenciar con precisión entre las masas benignas y las malignas en la mamografía y la ecografía es una cuestión de diagnóstico clínico que presenta una considerable variabilidad entre observadores. En este artículo se analizan los estudios publicados entre 2023 y 2026 que evalúan el rendimiento de los sistemas de inteligencia artificial (IA), con su complejo de «aprendizaje profundo», para ayudar a diferenciar entre masa benigna y masa maligna. Se realizó una búsqueda estructurada en PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect e IEEE Xplore. La evidencia disponible indica que los sistemas de deep learning alcanzan sensibilidades combinadas cercanas a 0,92–0,93 y especificidades de 0,88–0,91 en ecografía mamaria, mientras que en mamografía los valores de AUC en estudios de lectura se sitúan entre 0,87 y 0,90. Las técnicas multimodales que combinan información procedente de diferentes fuentes parecen tener mejor capacidad discriminativa en términos técnicos, aunque esto depende por completo del diseño del estudio y del grupo de pacientes estudiado. La mayoría de los estudios son retrospectivos, de un único centro y carecen de una validación externa prospectiva. Por lo tanto, parece que la inteligencia artificial podría resultar útil como apoyo en la práctica radiológica, pero aún se necesitan estudios prospectivos y multicéntricos para demostrar su precisión, así como un análisis detallado de sus implicaciones éticas y legales.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Distillation and Mutual Distillation Across Parallel Worlds of Large Language Models
abstract: Knowledge distillation is an important approach for transferring behavioral and predictive knowledge between neural networks. Recent work on large language models (LLMs) has investigated self-distillation, online knowledge distillation, adaptive teacher selection, and collaborative learning. However, a general framework that jointly organizes directional diversity among multiple descendants of a shared LLM, adaptive switching between self-distillation and mutual distillation, and optional participation by heterogeneous external LLMs remains a promising research direction requiring systematic investigation. This paper proposes Adaptive Parallel-World Distillation (APWD), a framework in which multiple learning branches originate from the same base LLM but pursue different distillation objectives, knowledge emphases, or learning trajectories. Each branch can independently perform self-distillation, while multiple branches can exchange knowledge through mutual distillation. An adaptive controller selects among self-distillation, mutual distillation, and hybrid distillation according to estimated learning progress, predictive uncertainty, complementary knowledge, knowledge-transfer compatibility, computational cost, and stability constraints. The framework can also incorporate external LLMs with different architectures, parameter scales, training histories, or capabilities. Unlike a fixed teacher–student pipeline, APWD treats the distillation relationship itself as an adaptive decision. The proposed design includes branch-specific objectives, confidence-aware teacher weighting, transfer-compatibility estimation, a constrained switching policy, and mechanisms for preserving useful diversity. We formalize the framework, present a training algorithm, identify research hypotheses, and design an experimental protocol covering reasoning, knowledge-intensive question answering, mathematical problem solving, and code generation. Because the framework has not yet been experimentally evaluated in this paper, its effectiveness and advantages over existing methods remain empirical questions rather than established results.

We formalize the framework, present a training algorithm, identify research hypotheses, and design an experimental protocol covering reasoning, knowledge-intensive question answering, mathematical problem solving, and code generation. Because the framework has not yet been experimentally evaluated in this paper, its effectiveness and advantages over existing methods remain empirical questions rather than established results.

title: Prospective replication of budget dependent evaluation inflation in evolutionary feature selection
abstract: This prospectively specified same-team replication tests three previously identified effects on eight non-biomedical UCI benchmark sources not used in the project's recorded earlier analyses. Structural qualification inspected source provenance, finite values, class counts and exact feature-vector repetitions. No new-study learner or search performance outcome has been generated. Historical published scores in official dataset descriptions may have been visible. The fixed design is eight tasks, five searches (GA, BPSO, binary DE, NSGA-II and ordinary random search), ridge and 5-NN, ten repetitions of five-fold outer CV, five inner folds and passive checkpoints at 250, 1,000 and 4,000 charged requests. Existing scientific implementations and hyperparameters are frozen. Inner standardization uses each inner training fold only. Published fixed numerical representations define the target; exact predictor-vector repetitions retain their first source row, and a predetermined stratified 1,200-row cap applies to Spambase and Gisette. The three primary estimands are dataset-level budget-gap growth from 250 to 4,000 requests, GA-ridge relative-advantage discrepancy against ordinary request-matched random search at 4,000, and the corresponding NSGA-II-5-NN discrepancy. Differences are paired within outer runs before averaging; the eight datasets receive equal weight. Report ordinary 95% and fixed three-item Bonferroni family intervals (98.333333% each; Student-t with seven degrees of freedom). Report every contrast, including partial or absent support. Do not pool old and new datasets or expand the collection to obtain significance. The exact protocol, 4,000-job freeze, raw and processed data, source code, dependency lock and 28 successful synthetic tests are in X11c_preregistration_c0aca37a692f.zip. title: Zero-Shot Spoken Language Understanding with SLAM-ASR: What Do Monolingual ASR-Trained Linear Projectors Enable?
abstract: The SLAM-ASR framework connects the features of a frozen speech encoder as input to a frozen LLM decoder to enable speech transcription. In this work we ask whether this training-on speech transcription-provides the LLM with the capability to also perform spoken language understanding (SLU) tasks, by training monolingual projectors on 11 languages. When prompted to answer a yes/no question about the input speech, the mean instruction following rate (IFR) is 49.8%. When not following the instruction, these models default back to transcription. The transcription quality-measured by the character error rate (CER)-is not sufficient to predict IFR. Remarkably, when the model is instructed to answer the topic question as a single digit option, the mean IFR rises to 81.3%. Our models score a mean 23.2% topic balanced accuracy (BAcc) against 14.3% chance. However, the same decoder scores a mean 71.5% BAcc when using reference transcripts as text input. This indicates a failure of the projector to transfer information for the SLU tasks.

title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention
abstract: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.

title: Quantifying Annotation Agreement in Object Detection with Optimal Transport
abstract: Reliable validation of machine learning models is a crucial step in designing robust and trustworthy systems. Yet validation relies on annotated test sets treated as ground truth, even though annotations can be noisy or ambiguous. In object detection, sources may disagree on object presence, box location, or class label. Standard agreement metrics usually binarize box overlap before computing a summary score, obscuring the degree and structure of disagreement between annotation sets. Here, we study an Optimal Transport (OT)-based metric for measuring agreement between object detection annotations. Instead of binarizing bounding box overlap, this metric assigns graded costs to matched and unmatched labeled boxes. Through theoretical analysis and experiments on real and synthetically perturbed annotations, we show that OT captures graded changes in agreement and distinguishes annotation pairs that thresholded metrics score identically. Our results suggest that OT provides a richer measure of annotation agreement in object detection, especially for domains with many small or ambiguous objects. Such agreement estimates can support more reliable validation when labels are noisy or conflicting.

title: SceneAE: Scene Generation and Reconstruction in Queryable 3D-Anchored Latent Space
abstract: Recent video world models have increasingly adopted 3D memory mechanisms to integrate historical observations into a lightweight and persistent scene representation. This naturally raises a complementary question: if 3D representations can serve as an effective mechanism for memorizing observed scenes, can they also be directly used as the latent space for reconstructing and generating scenes? Motivated by this idea, we represent a scene as a compact and unstructured 3D-anchored latent space (\textbf{SceneAE}). Each latent combines an explicit 3D position with an implicit content feature and is spatially grounded to describe its local scene region, forming a sparse latent point cloud. Unlike conventional video-VAE latents that describe how a scene appears from particular viewpoints, our representation directly describes the scene itself, making it naturally applicable to both reconstruction and generation. For reconstruction, once the scene has been generated, our persistent 3D representation can be projected and decoded into RGB-D observations by different target cameras, without the need to regenerate a video for each new camera trajectory. For generation, we leverage the geometry-content separation to first generate camera-controlled 3D geometry and then synthesize content conditioned on it, reducing camera-appearance entanglement and improving camera controllability. Experiments show that this 3D latent achieves superior generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.

title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? Resolution-Dependent Interaction Order and Computational Capacity
abstract: Mandlebrot's coastline paradox reframes measurement as a joint property of an object and its ruler. Here we ask how observational resolution shapes the apparent structure of neural computation. We introduce a scale-indexed decomposition that separates the predictive information captured by direct dependencies from the residual outside that model family. Exact constructions show that projection can convert higher-order dependence into pairwise structure. Projection can increase the direct fraction of surviving information even as total predictive information decreases. A schematic branch-to-soma cascade grounds these effects in local coincidence detection, saturating integration and somatic mixing. Resolving organized nonlinear subunits improves approximation and raises effective representational rank. In a nested hierarchy, these gains occur without increasing information about the target. This distinction separates information availability from access by a restricted readout. A point-neuron or direct population model therefore establishes an effective description at a specified scale. It does not uniquely identify the finer computation that generated the observed relation. Which resolution is adequate depends on the observable and perturbation of interest.

title: Efficient routing and spectrum allocation in arbitrary flex-grid entanglement networks
abstract: As practical quantum networks approach large-scale deployment, the need for efficient user-to-user frequency allocation is increasing, yet current approaches only provide partial solutions to the routing and spectrum allocation problem for an arbitrary quantum network. We address this challenge for repeater-less flex-grid quantum networks based on hyperentangled photons using an efficient three-stage pipeline combining leading tools in classical networking with recent advances in numerical optimization. First, double instantiations of Yen's algorithm obtain low-loss route candidates between each pair of users and the entanglement sources. Second, the advanced process optimizer (APOPT) obtains frequency channel allocations that maximize distribution rates under fidelity constraints. Finally, the constraint programming solver using satisfiability methods (CP-SAT) assigns specific frequency bins to each link, ensuring that there is no contention between frequencies from different sources. We numerically demonstrate this approach on a representative ring network and a Manhattan incumbent local exchange carrier topology, realizing significant improvements over prior genetic algorithm approaches in speed, accuracy, and scalability. Overall, this pipeline provides an efficient heuristic workflow for optimizing broadband entanglement distribution, applicable to arbitrarily connected quantum networks integrated within the existing lightwave infrastructure.

title: Conceptual Neural Networks 2.0: A Distributed Cognitive Architecture for Conceptual Reasoning, Controlled Neuroplasticity, Collaborative Intelligence, and Ethical Governance
abstract: Artificial intelligence has achieved significant progress in pattern recognition, language generation, multimodal processing, and automated problem-solving. However, the increasing capabilities of individual models do not necessarily translate into coherent, persistent, adaptable, or ethically governed artificial reasoning systems. This paper presents Conceptual Neural Networks 2.0 (CNN 2.0), an evolution of a conceptual architecture initially proposed to move beyond isolated statistical representations toward structured conceptual entities, explicit relationships, contextual reasoning, and ethical decision-making. Despite its name, CNN 2.0 is not a new neural network topology: Conceptual Neural Networks is the name of a cognitive architecture framework. CNN 2.0 extends the original conceptual framework into a distributed cognitive architecture composed of specialized agents, permanent and dynamic conceptual groups, a controlled orchestration mechanism, distributed memory, uncertainty management, autonomous inquiry and discovery, and controlled structural adaptation. Its central research question is how to design an artificial system that can not only reason, but also recognize the limits of its knowledge, investigate its own deficiencies, reorganize its capabilities, and remain subject to rules it cannot modify unilaterally. The paper makes two central contributions. The first is an explicit architectural separation between cognitive capability and operational authority, formalized as an authorization model with default deny, data-dependent risk classification, bounded human delegation, and enforcement by an Ethical Governance and Authorization Layer (EGAL) that operates outside the components it governs. The second is governed structural adaptation: a Cognitive Neuroplasticity Engine (CNE) proposes changes to agents, groups, and relationships, while a versioned Cognitive Genome separates a mutable structural layer from a protected normative layer and enforces explicit invariants. These contributions are integrated with a Cognitive Inquiry and Discovery Engine (CIDE), a Cognitive Uncertainty Manager (CUM), a Cognitive Link Manager (CLM), the Domain Factory, and a memory model with explicit epistemic status. Governance follows eleven principles of ethical resolution, organized as constitutional commitments, principles of evaluation and decision, and epistemic and procedural safeguards. The paper defines verifiable architectural properties, a threat model, an integrated operating scenario, the current implementation status in three production domains, and a validation methodology. The architecture adopts the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol for communication between agents and adds two layers on top of it: verified capability profiles, measured by the network rather than declared by each agent, and EGAL authorization in front of every agent call. Quantum-inspired reasoning remains an optional research direction. The paper does not claim that the complete architecture has been implemented or experimentally validated: the governance and adaptation mechanisms (EGAL, CNE, and the Cognitive Genome) are specified but not yet implemented, the properties the paper states are design requirements until tested, and no performance advantage over existing architectures is claimed.

title: Generative Structural Theory v1.15 — A Conditional Fibre Characterisation of a Provenance-Population Condition and a Recorded Verdict
abstract: GST v1.14 found, on a fixed single-arc census record, that a provenance-population condition Q_D selects a non-empty set strictly inside the set of candidates whose recorded verdict is the E1 word (E_rec). This note describes what the two conditions require. For each candidate in a stated range, the full and prefix chain-tuple sets F_a and P_a are finite and componentwise truncation is a map rho_a : F_a -> P_a; with b_a the surplus of the fibres over the image and h_a the number of empty fibres, |F_a| - |P_a| = b_a - h_a, a statement about finite sets and maps. Assuming the provenance premise PR (that the record lines were produced by the specified code on the specified inputs and were not changed after generation) and the correspondence between these objects and the census implementation, established by drafting-side static matching and reading, Q_D holds on the domain D exactly when b_a > h_a, and E_rec holds exactly when the code's prefix condition prefix_ok holds (the code's test, not the census rule's whole prefix clause), some letter index has an extra level, and F_a is non-empty. This gives a conditional characterisation of the difference between the two conditions by the fibres of rho_a: under Q_D, E_rec reduces to prefix_ok; E_rec without Q_D falls into exactly one of two cases (rho_a injective, or non-injective with at least as many empty fibres as the surplus). Which concrete fibre structure produced the strict inclusion on the fixed record is not determined. The result is conditional on PR, which is not verified; it does not resolve single-arc eligibility; and it does not identify the mechanism by which the difference arises on the record.

title: Research drafts on revl: typed revertible effects, replay, hot swap and agent authority
abstract: 68 research paper drafts about revl, a language and compiler for agent systems built on the Cordis plugin framework. Topics: typed revertible effects, space and time replay, generational hot swap across runtimes, emergency stop, capability-bound secrets, information flow from untrusted data, a self-hosted compiler checked against a differential oracle, and governed self-evolution of agents. Each draft gives its claim, its contributions, related work, the evidence on revl main with file and line references, the numbers measured so far, a paper outline and its threats to validity. The claims were checked against revl commit 45bec431f3216bdcc0cda97981f2c4830dced3a3. These are drafts, not peer reviewed. The archive holds the Markdown sources (papers/, README.md, research.json) and the rendered HTML pages (html/research/index.html). The same pages are published at https://inso1337.github.io/revl/research/.

title: Forget Gradient Surgery: A Characterization of Projected Gradient Descent for Graph Edge Unlearning
abstract: Preprint of the paper 'Forget Gradient Surgery: A Characterization of Projected Gradient Descent for Graph Edge Unlearning' (submitted to TMLR). Machine unlearning for graph neural networks is complicated by message passing: deleting an edge from the adjacency matrix does not erase what the parameters learned from it, and naive gradient ascent on the forgotten edges degrades performance on the rest of the graph. We study Forget Gradient Surgery (FGS), an approximate edge-unlearning method that combines a forget direction defined as the gradient of the forgotten-edge link logits under the post-deletion adjacency, an orthogonal projection against a deterministic retain anchor, and a data-driven stopping rule. Evaluated against retrain-from-scratch on Cora, CiteSeer, and PubMed (n = 10 seeds each) across deletion fractions 1%-20%, with link-inference attack AUC as the forgetting metric and held-out link AUC as utility, we find a Pareto frontier rather than a single winner: the KS-stopped variant is 2.3-2.7x faster than retraining and not significantly different from retrain on PubMed (attack gap +0.002, p = 0.40) and Cora (attack gap +0.008, p = 0.19), but under-forgets on CiteSeer (attack gap +0.037) and collapses at 20% deletion on Cora (utility -0.055). An attack-calibrated stopping variant closes the CiteSeer gap (paired improvement +0.028, p < 0.001) at the cost of up to 2x retraining time. A matched no-projection ablation shows the projection causally preserves utility (Cora -0.048, p < 0.001, dz = -2.51) while naive ascent destroys it.

An attack-calibrated stopping variant closes the CiteSeer gap (paired improvement +0.028, p < 0.001) at the cost of up to 2x retraining time. A matched no-projection ablation shows the projection causally preserves utility (Cora -0.048, p < 0.001, dz = -2.51) while naive ascent destroys it.

title: Practical wavelength selection for quantum-augmented networks over shared optical fiber
abstract: In a quantum augmented network, sharing optical fiber with classical traffic requires quantum wavelength selection to balance logical fidelity, block acceptance, and classical data reception. Here we develop a wavelength-selection framework for an error-corrected three-stage quantum communication protocol. Under a thermal-background model with independent errors, an ideal one-photon receiver, and ideal recovery, we derive an accepted qubit channel and a key-independent lower bound on logical entanglement fidelity. Combining this bound with block acceptance gives an entanglement-fidelity yield bound, which we maximize over evaluated wavelengths subject to fidelity and classical link-budget requirements. For the Steane [[7,1,3]] code at 5 km per traversal and -10 dBm per classical channel, the largest fidelity certificate occurs near 1537 nm, whereas the largest yield bound occurs near 1551 nm. Along the 1.25 Gb/s classical link budget with 0.2% base error, the optimized yield bound falls below 10^-6 near 10 km per traversal, while fidelity remains certified at 0.99 or higher at longer spans. These results distinguish fidelity and yield constraints and identify certified operating regions for quantum-augmented networks sharing optical fiber.

title: EarlyCommit: Calibrated Word-by-Word Commitment for Robots Acting Before You Finish Speaking
abstract: Human listeners can often identify the intended object several words before an instruction ends. Robots, however, are typically designed to wait until the speaker has finished before deciding how to act. We present EarlyCommit, an open-source tool that lets a robot commit to the intended object while the instruction is being spoken. After every recognized word, a fine-tuned text encoder scores each object in the scene. The robot acts when the calibrated probability of the best object reaches a threshold tau set by the user, so 1 - tau is the accepted risk of choosing the wrong object. Otherwise, it waits or asks. The tool includes a streaming speech front end, a scene and instruction generator with exact word-by-word ground truth, and scripts to train, calibrate, and evaluate. On instructions containing words never seen in training, EarlyCommit commits correctly 1.6 to 2 times as often as keyword matching, is right at least 92 percent of the time when it commits at tau = 0.9, and needs 31 to 35 ms per word on consumer GPUs.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning with Receding-Horizon Safety Critic and Differentiable Action Shields
abstract: Despite the Markov assumption, safety failures in robot reinforcement learning rarely occur instantaneously; they typically emerge over several steps as the policy enters unfamiliar states under disturbances and domain shift. We address this limitation by learning a receding-horizon safety critic that predicts whether a state will remain non-terminating over the next receding horizon, enabling anticipatory detection of impending locomotion failures. The critic is trained from rollout-derived horizon labels with a composite objective that combines horizon classification, control-barrier-function-inspired temporal consistency, and smoothness regularization, and we aggregate an ensemble of critics with a conservative Conditional Value at Risk estimate to account for uncertainty. Building on the learned critic, we derive a closed-form, differentiable CBF-style safety filter that minimally modifies the policy action to improve predicted safety, and integrate it into PPO with an anticipation loss to reduce policy-filter mismatch during training. In simulated quadruped locomotion, our method improves robustness under action noise, external perturbations, and terrain shifts, reducing catastrophic failures while maintaining competitive returns.
