title: Mixed Poisson diffusion models and application to posterior sampling
abstract: Diffusion models are a powerful framework for learning complex probability distributions. While widely used diffusion models for continuous data rely on Gaussian noising processes, we instead develop diffusion models based on Poisson noise. More precisely, we introduce and study a new mathematical framework, called Mixed Poisson Diffusion Models (MPDM), with noising dynamics driven by multivariate counting processes. Our methodology is motivated by Poisson inverse problems. The success of Gaussian diffusion models has led to their use as prior models in a growing number of posterior sampling methods for inverse problems. However, most of these approaches focus on Gaussian inverse problems, in which observations are generated through a deterministic forward operator corrupted by additive Gaussian noise. By contrast, Poisson inverse problems, where observations are discrete and Poisson distributed, remain comparatively underexplored in this literature. Building on our Poisson generative dynamics, we develop a natural framework for posterior sampling in Poisson inverse problems and derive several posterior sampling algorithms based on the proposed model. We evaluate our approach on realistic Poisson inverse problems and show that the resulting framework is well suited to this class of problems.

title: Joint-measurement advantage and finite-time transitions in accelerated detector registers
abstract: The Unruh response thermalizes accelerated detectors, but the entanglement remaining in a register does not by itself specify what distributed measurements can recover. We study this distinction for a four-qubit cluster state whose two assisting nodes independently undergo generalized amplitude damping, while the target nodes remain isolated and the environments are inaccessible. We derive the exact joint-assisted concurrence and the exact one-way value for arbitrary local measurements. The joint optimum equals the bipartition negativity, and computational-basis measurements attain the one-way optimum. A polar-decomposition argument, together with compactness, establishes a necessary and sufficient condition for separable measurements to attain the joint optimum and proves a strict gap whenever this condition fails. For assisting detectors at equal Unruh temperature with relaxation-rate ratio $r>1$, joint advantage exists precisely when the thermal excitation factor satisfies $q<1/r$. At finite positive temperature it ends at a unique finite time, while the remaining entanglement is nonzero. For $r=2$, both the transition time and remaining resource have closed expressions. These results identify when joint assistance is necessary within the independent weak-coupling thermalization model.

title: Verifying deployed bytecode against executable EVM semantics, with exact gas and no added axioms
abstract: Much of Ethereum's most consequential code is immutable bytecode: old output of unverified compilers, and protocol logic run as contract code. We show that such bytecode can be verified as it is, without trusting what produced it, without simplifying the machine it runs on, and with no axioms beyond Lean's own. Blanc, a Lean 4 verification stack, reads fixed runtime bytes via kernel-checked certificates and states every theorem against Jaune, an executable semantics of the EVM and block processing that passes all 34,205 blockchain-test cases of Ethereum's fixture release v20.0.2 that involve only forks that have governed mainnet since May 2025. Eight artifacts, deployed from 2017 to 2026, come from seven compiler versions and an assembler. For the EIP-7002 contract, we prove that the end-of-block call to it, whose failure would invalidate the block, succeeds whatever its storage holds, and that each block's withdrawal requests are exactly the oldest pending submissions; mainnet met these theorems' starting premises when Prague began. For a Uniswap V2 pair, we prove that after any valid history whose hashed slots stay apart, from any checkpoint representing its Solidity model's state, the storage represents that model replayed over exactly the committed calls, a balanced liquidity ledger stays balanced, and, under a premise on token answers, geometric-mean reserves per share fall only through the protocol fee. Exact gas makes liveness provable: a tracked WETH9 holder without code can withdraw by a transaction whose gas has a closed form, matching all 3,748 comparable mainnet receipts of its shape in 30,000 blocks. On Curve pool bytes compiled with the lock bug exploited in 2023, Jaune executes such a reentrancy from deployment; for bytes from a fixed compiler, we prove the lock excludes it. AI agents wrote the proofs in fifteen days under one author's direction, atop an existing stack.

title: State-Matched Sequence Conformal Prediction
abstract: Sequential conformal prediction needs to decide which past errors should calibrate uncertainty for the current target. Recency and online error feedback are useful when recent observations remain relevant, but the recent past can be a poor reference when comparable states recur at nonadjacent times, with the recurrence pattern generally unknown. We propose State-Matched Sequence Conformal Prediction (SMSCP), which constructs an explicit one-sided local-linear state from pre-target information, uses state similarity to select a matched reference set of past calibration scores, and then applies the ordinary unweighted conformal order statistic. In contrast to existing approaches, SMSCP uses state similarity to identify calibration observations relevant to the target score quantile. This motivates a theoretical analysis of whether nearby states have comparable target score quantiles under temporal dependence. We establish control of the resulting conformal cutoff and characterize predictive information not captured by the chosen state. Simulations show that state matching is most effective when score-relevant states recur across nonadjacent times, while revealing settings in which its advantage weakens or reverses. Across solar irradiance and bike-demand benchmarks, SMSCP improves interval score over recency, weighted, adaptive, and HopCPT comparators, and achieves coverage closer to the nominal 0.90 level than ResCP on five of six benchmarks.

title: Securing the Retrieval-Augmented Generation Pipeline: A Multi-Layered Defense Architecture Against Hallucinations and Prompt Injection Attacks
abstract: The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into enterprise applications has exposed critical safety vulnerabilities, most notably hallucinations and prompt injection attacks. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) was introduced to ground LLMs in external knowledge, it inadvertently expands the attack surface. This paper proposes a Multi-Layered Defense Architecture (MLDA) designed specifically to secure the RAG pipeline. Our framework introduces three sequential safety phases: Input Intent Verification, Contextual Grounding, and Output Confidence Filtering. To empirically validate the feasibility of the Output Confidence Filtering phase, we deployed a lightweight, open-source Natural Language Inference (NLI) model (BART-large-MNLI) to detect factual contradictions simulating LLM hallucinations. Experimental results demonstrate that the NLI model successfully identifies factual discrepancies with high confidence scores ranging from 0.82 to 0.97. This research provides a practical, reproducible, and mathematically agnostic safety framework for deploying LLMs in sensitive environments without relying on computationally expensive retraining.

title: Parallel-World Adaptive Self-Memory and Shared-Memory Switching for Large Language Models
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory to support long-term interaction, task continuity, experience reuse, and collaborative problem-solving. However, existing memory architectures often emphasize individual memory management, shared memory repositories, or predefined collaboration strategies. These approaches leave an important design question: how can multiple memory perspectives generated by the same model coexist with memories maintained by heterogeneous models, while the system adaptively determines when to operate independently and when to exchange information? This paper proposes Parallel-World Adaptive Self-Memory and Shared-Memory Switching (PW-ASMS), a unified framework that combines parallel memory worlds, adaptive self-memory, shared-memory collaboration, and cross-model memory integration. Parallel memory worlds are created by assigning different memory orientations to instances of the same underlying model. Each world independently selects, organizes, updates, and retrieves experiences according to its designated orientation. A dynamic controller subsequently determines whether an agent should rely on its own memory, exchange information with other parallel worlds, consult a shared memory repository, or combine these operations. The framework also supports heterogeneous LLMs whose memories can contribute complementary information to a common collaborative process. The proposed architecture consists of parallel memory worlds, individual memory stores, a governed shared memory layer, a memory evaluation module, and an adaptive switching controller. A utility-based decision mechanism considers task relevance, information novelty, confidence, memory consistency, communication cost, privacy constraints, and expected downstream benefit. The framework is designed to reduce unnecessary information exchange while preserving opportunities for collaborative knowledge acquisition. We formulate research questions, operational procedures, evaluation metrics, and experimental comparisons to assess its effectiveness. The paper provides a conceptual and methodological foundation for investigating adaptive memory organization in multi-agent LLM systems; its effectiveness remains to be established empirically.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Supervision and Collaborative Supervision for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate their own supervision signals, evaluate their intermediate outputs, and learn from automatically constructed training examples. Multiple LLMs can also provide supervision to one another by exchanging predictions, explanations, critiques, and candidate labels. However, relying exclusively on self-supervision may preserve individual model errors, whereas relying continuously on collaborative supervision may introduce correlated errors, unnecessary communication costs, and dependence on other models. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching between Self-Supervision and Collaborative Supervision (ASSCS), a framework in which multiple LLMs dynamically select between independent supervision and cross-model supervision according to the estimated reliability, uncertainty, disagreement, computational cost, and expected learning benefit of each mode. Unlike a fixed self-supervision strategy or a permanently collaborative strategy, ASSCS treats the supervision mode as a dynamic decision variable. Each model can supervise its own learning when its evidence is sufficiently reliable, request supervision from selected peer models when additional evidence is valuable, and return to self-supervision when collaboration offers insufficient benefit. The framework incorporates a supervision reliability estimator, a mode-selection policy, a peer-selection mechanism, a consistency-aware learning objective, and a cost-sensitive switching rule. This paper formalizes the proposed mechanism, describes an implementable training algorithm, identifies theoretical conditions under which adaptive switching may improve the quality-cost trade-off, and presents an empirical evaluation protocol. The proposed framework is intended to investigate whether adaptive supervision allocation can improve learning reliability and efficiency across heterogeneous LLMs. Its effectiveness remains an empirical question requiring systematic comparison with fixed-mode and existing collaborative learning methods.

title: A Transformer Based Model to Detect Environmental Related Distress on Online Social Media
abstract: Online social media has been recently employed as the source of data for the detection of traffic-related activities and to control the flow of traffic in smart cities all over the world. Till now an ample amount of research work has been done in identification of traffic-related incidents with the help of online social media platforms (mostly Twitter). Along with the problem of traffic the society face the problem of increase in pollution and its related health hazards. Online social media proved to be effective in correctly mapping the sentiments of the people suffering from the problem of pollution with the exact measure of the harmful substances in the air. In this work, we presented a novel approach for analysing the environment-related distress on online social media related to pollution using BERT based transformer. In this paper we analysed the tweets and classified them into two classes: i) Pollution specific, ii) Location Specific by using the machine learning algorithms. From the location-specific tweets about the pollution, we then identify the location with serious pollution-related issues. The model was trained and evaluated on a dataset of 21,549 geotagged tweets collected from Delhi over a one-year period (January 2019–January 2020). The proposed BERT-based classifier achieved an accuracy of 96.5% and an F1-score of 96%, outperforming baseline machine learning algorithms and existing BERT-based benchmarks. Unlike prior BERT-based sentiment models that focus on general positive/negative polarity, our approach is specifically fine-tuned to detect pollution-related environmental distress and integrates geographic information extraction to identify urban pollution hotspots. This dual classification into Pollution Specific (PS) and Location Specific (LS) categories enables direct, actionable outputs for urban planners and traffic management authorities. The findings carry direct implications for smart city governance, enabling authorities to identify pollution hotspots and design data-driven interventions including traffic rerouting and targeted public health alerts.

From the location-specific tweets about the pollution, we then identify the location with serious pollution-related issues. The model was trained and evaluated on a dataset of 21,549 geotagged tweets collected from Delhi over a one-year period (January 2019–January 2020). The proposed BERT-based classifier achieved an accuracy of 96.5% and an F1-score of 96%, outperforming baseline machine learning algorithms and existing BERT-based benchmarks. Unlike prior BERT-based sentiment models that focus on general positive/negative polarity, our approach is specifically fine-tuned to detect pollution-related environmental distress and integrates geographic information extraction to identify urban pollution hotspots. This dual classification into Pollution Specific (PS) and Location Specific (LS) categories enables direct, actionable outputs for urban planners and traffic management authorities. The findings carry direct implications for smart city governance, enabling authorities to identify pollution hotspots and design data-driven interventions including traffic rerouting and targeted public health alerts.

title: Proactive AI Support and Student Learning: A Retrospective Record of a Randomized Study
abstract: This registration documents a completed nine-week study of proactive versus student-initiated AI learning support. Within 18 university classes, 480 undergraduate students were assigned to four conditions in a 2 × 2 design combining support initiation (proactive or student-initiated) with EEG-summary availability (available or unavailable). The study examined self-regulated learning, course-task performance, performance when AI support was temporarily withdrawn, and transfer to new tasks completed without AI. It also examined daily learning records, AI interaction events, EEG-derived features, and a later evaluative-judgement assessment. This record describes the study design, outcome definitions, and analyses reported in the manuscript. It was prepared after data collection and analysis; it is not a prospective preregistration.

title: When emotions matter: the contextual effectiveness of emotional expressions in AI agents
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) agents’ emotional expressions (positive or neutral) interact with service task types (subjective or objective) to shape consumer service satisfaction, and explore the mediating roles of mind perception, including perceived agency and perceived experience, in this process. Design/methodology/approach This work uses four studies, including a secondary data analysis of relevant Weibo posts and three scenario experiments involving a total of 587 participants, to underline the interaction effect between AI agents’ emotional expressions and service tasks on service satisfaction, and demonstrate the dual-path mediating effect of mind perception. Findings Across four studies, the authors find that the effectiveness of AI agents’ emotional expressions depends on service task characteristics. The secondary data analysis of Weibo posts first documents consumers’ differential responses to AI emotional expressions across subjective and objective service contexts. Three scenario experiments then establish that positive emotional expressions are more effective for subjective tasks, whereas neutral emotional expressions are more effective for objective tasks. Further analyses show that these effects operate through distinct psychological pathways: positive emotions enhance perceived experience in subjective tasks, whereas neutral emotions strengthen perceived agency in objective tasks, ultimately increasing consumer satisfaction. Research limitations/implications This study, while strong in internal validity, faces external validity limitations. It focuses on AI communication in commercial service texts, neglecting other domains like education and health care, and overlooking the nonverbal emotional expressions of embodied AI. In addition, the research primarily uses service satisfaction as the sole dependent variable, thus missing a broader spectrum of consumer responses such as repurchase intentions and word-of-mouth. Practical implications This research informs managers that AI service agents should be designed as social actors with mind perception rather than as purely functional tools. Firms can leverage emotional expressions to shape consumers’ social evaluations of AI. But emotional design should align with service task types: positive emotional cues are more effective for subjective, experiential tasks, whereas neutral styles better support objective, data-driven tasks. Originality/value This study contributes to the emotional AI literature by uncovering critical situational factors that shape the effectiveness of AI emotional expressions and advances the authors’ understanding of the underlying mechanisms through a dual-path mediation framework of mind perception. The findings also provide practical implications for the strategic deployment of emotional AI in service design.

title: Probing Negation Understanding in Vision-Language Models With Object Attention
abstract: Negation is a fundamental aspect of language understanding and it is important vision-language models (VLMs) are able to process it effectively. We investigate how VLMs process negation by analysing attention patterns of different models. We draw comparisons between human gaze and attention in models when processing affirmative vs negated statements. We compare object level model attention to human eye-fixations in both binary and multary settings, evaluating with both synthetic and realistic datasets. We find models generally do not follow human-like attention patterns when resolving negation, suggesting they rely on mechanisms outside of attention. While layerwise analysis shows that PaliGemma2-3B shifts object attention to the alternative under negation, our headwise ablations suggest this is a byproduct rather than a negation processing mechanism. Additionally, we find that LLaVA-1.5-7B displays a spatial bias towards left-side objects. Our evaluation of models on downstream tasks shows that all models have a discrepancy between affirmative and negated questions highlighting the need to better understand the underlying processing of negation to close this performance gap. Code available at https://github.com/otmive/negation_attention

title: Learning by Examples: Power Grid Steady State Analysis with a Tabular Foundation Model
abstract: Foundation models have shown strong generalization across scientific domains, but their use in power systems remains largely task-specific. We investigate whether a pretrained tabular foundation model (TFM), TabPFN, can serve as a general-purpose neural solver for power grid steady-state analysis. We evaluate the TFM on three tasks: power flow (PF) prediction, N-k contingency screening (NCS), and voltage stability margin (VSM) prediction. We performed experiments on 118- and 2000-bus systems, comparing the TFM against task-specific neural baselines. Without retraining or fine-tuning, the TFM matches or outperforms the best task-specific model in several settings across the three tasks. For 118-bus PF prediction, a variant of the TFM achieves errors of $1\times 10^{-3}$ pu for voltage magnitudes and $0.30^\circ$ for voltage angles, outperforming all baselines. On unseen N-1 contingency and close-to-infeasible PF cases, the TFM is competitive with the DCPF approximation. For millions of unseen N-2 contingencies, the TFM achieves AUCs of 0.92 and 0.95 for branch and voltage violation screening, respectively. The TFM also attains accurate VSM prediction performance for the 2000-bus system with limited labelled data. The TFM attains strong results across the tested tasks despite pretraining without any power-system-specific dataset and requiring no fine-tuning step. These results offer a glimpse into the potential of pretrained TFMs as a neural solver for a range of power grid analysis tasks.

title: Continual pretraining Prostate MRI ViT Encoder for task alignment
abstract: Building foundation models for MRI has emerged as a promising direction for advancing medical image analysis and improving accessibility of task specific models. Existing approaches primarily focus on effective pretraining strategies and evaluating their performance across diverse downstream tasks. While these methods show performance gains, limited attention has been given to understanding task alignment between pretraining and downstream objectives. Unlike language models, where the two stages are naturally aligned, such alignment is less evident in vision based applications. Motivated by this gap, we explore continual pretraining. Specifically, continually pretraining a pretrained ViT encoder using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on a prostate segmentation task to enhance task alignment and downstream performance. We further perform layer-wise representational analysis using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) to assess representational shifts and their correlation with task outcomes. Our experiments show improved performance in 3 of 6 downstream tasks and comparable results in the others. Our Feature analysis reveals that, for segmentation tasks, continually pretrained encoder features exhibit greater similarity to those of the finetuned encoder than the original pretrained encoder, correlating with observed performance gains.

title: The Trust Paradox of AI-Generated Content Transparency: Impulse Buying from the Perspective of Generative Agents
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in digital e-commerce environments, the transparency labeling of AI-generated content has emerged as a crucial institutional variable in modern platform governance. Drawing upon the established information–trust–behavior theoretical logic, this study conducted a large-scale AI-agent simulation, comprising 900 distinct purchase decisions executed by large language model agents, to systematically test how disclosure labeling affects simulated consumer trust and simulated impulse buying intention. Furthermore, the research investigated whether trust acts as a mediating mechanism and whether consumer involvement moderates these relationships. Rigorous model-rationality validation confirmed that the agent decisions consistently conformed to their assigned behavioral personalities and rational economic logic. The empirical results demonstrated that disclosure labeling significantly suppressed both simulated trust and impulse buying intention. Additionally, simulated trust positively predicted impulse intention, revealing a negative indirect association within the disclosure–impulse behavioral link. Notably, consumer involvement moderated the trust–impulse path during the primary simulation phase, although this moderating effect was not replicated in the cross-model robustness check. Ultimately, these comprehensive findings reveal the critical boundary conditions of the institutional logic surrounding the exchange of transparency for trust. The study provides robust, simulation-based empirical evidence for the development of AI-content labeling policies and offers valuable insights for optimizing platform information governance strategies in the digital economy.

title: Adaptive Self–Mutual Mechanism Switching Across Heterogeneous Systems and Parallel Worlds: A General Framework for Dynamic Interaction, Coordination, and Adaptation
abstract: Systems operating in complex environments often rely on a limited set of predefined behavioral mechanisms, interaction patterns, or coordination strategies. Although existing research has extensively investigated self-adaptive systems, distributed coordination, system-of-systems engineering, and dynamic reconfiguration, a general challenge remains: how can a system dynamically determine whether to operate independently, interact with alternative realizations of itself, cooperate with heterogeneous systems, or combine multiple interaction modes according to changing conditions? This paper proposes the Adaptive Self–Mutual Mechanism Switching Framework (ASMSF), a general conceptual framework for adaptive interaction among arbitrary systems. The framework is not restricted to artificial intelligence, machine learning, software, or any particular technical domain. It encompasses computational systems, physical systems, organizational systems, industrial processes, and other systems whose states, actions, and interactions can be meaningfully represented. The framework introduces three principal interaction scopes: self-directed mechanisms within an individual system, interaction among parallel-world realizations of the same underlying system, and interaction among heterogeneous or otherwise distinct systems. Parallel worlds are defined as alternative realizations of a common system under different configurations, objectives, assumptions, environmental conditions, or developmental trajectories. An adaptive controller selects, switches, combines, or terminates mechanisms according to expected performance, uncertainty, resource expenditure, interaction benefits, and operational constraints. Rather than prescribing a fixed sequence of self-operation followed by collaboration, ASMSF treats interaction mode selection as a continuing decision problem. It proposes a common representation for mechanism selection, a cost-sensitive switching policy, a parallel-world coordination procedure, and a cross-system interoperability layer. A research agenda is presented to evaluate the framework against fixed-mode, threshold-based, and adaptive baselines. The principal contribution is a unified, domain-independent formulation of adaptive self–mutual interaction across alternative realizations and heterogeneous systems. Its effectiveness and novelty as a complete implementation remain empirical questions requiring comparative experiments and systematic literature review.

title: STRUCTURAL, GEOCHEMICAL AND GIS CRITERIA FOR PREDICTING LEAD–ZINC MINERALIZATION IN THE GILON PROSPECT, SOUTHERN UZBEKISTAN
abstract: The Gilon prospect in the Hissar Mountains of southern Uzbekistan is officially listed as a prospective polymetallic area with copper, zinc and lead resource indicators. This thesis summarizes exploration criteria for Pb–Zn mineralization by integrating regional metallogenic analogues, structural geology, mineralogy, geochemistry and GIS-based targeting. The well-studied Khandiza Zn–Pb–Cu–Ag system is used as a regional methodological analogue rather than as a direct genetic equivalent. Priority targets are expected where favorable volcanic-sedimentary or reactive carbonate lithologies coincide with fault intersections, hydrothermal alteration and multi-element Pb–Zn–Cu–Ag anomalies.

title: Weather-Driven Solar Intensity Forecasting for Smart Homes : A Comparative Machine Learning Study
abstract: Solar intensity forecasting can help residential photovoltaic systems anticipate solar availability and plan electricity use. This paper presents a detailed account of the approach described in the supplied seminar report, which predicts global horizontal irradiance (GHI) using weather-related variables. The reported pipeline includes data cleaning, normalization, correlation analysis, an 80:20 training-test split, and a comparison of conventional machine-learning algorithms with a fully connected neural network. The considered models are Linear Regression, Quadratic Regression, Naive Bayes, k-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), and a neural network. The report records the lowest mean squared error (MSE) for the neural network at 1,675.94, followed by KNN at 2,587.07. These results indicate that the neural network performed best among the evaluated alternatives in the reported experiment. Some dataset and training details are not specified sufficiently for exact reproduction; therefore, the paper presents the reported findings without claiming independent implementation or validation.

title: How requests change the diversity of LLM answers (confirmatory study)
abstract: This is the plan for a confirmatory study of how the wording of a request changes the diversity of answers from large language models (LLMs). Six LLMs see the same beginning of a list of animals or foods written by people. They are then asked for one more item, a closely related item, an item from a different group, or an uncommon item, each in three wordings. We test whether asking for something different brings back the models' usual answers, and whether asking for something closely related leads away from them. A secondary experiment repeats the test in two idea-generation tasks. Data will be generated only after this plan is registered.

title: Geltungs-Prüfkunde: Endliche Gegenmodelle und Schlussprüfung. Band 2
abstract: Geltungs-Prüfkunde Band 2 enthält 200 deutsch-englische Bereichsdefinitionen zu endlichen Gegenmodellen und Schlussprüfung. Beispiele, Gegenfälle und Grenzen sind deutsch und ausdrücklich konstruiert. Zehn Module behandeln Argumente, Operatoren, Tabellen, Gegenmodellsuche, Prämissenänderung, Äquivalenzregeln, Herleitung, Ausdrucksbäume, endliche Funktionsrelationen und Prüfbelege. Mit KI-Unterstützung ausgearbeitete Arbeitsfassung; bekannte Logik wird nicht als historische Erfindung, neue Disziplin oder gemessene Wirkung ausgegeben. Volume 2 contains 200 paired German-English scoped working definitions. An original classical Boolean tree evaluator represents all 16 two-atom truth functions, compares 256 ordered function pairs by direct valuation and model-set inclusion, and checks 4,096 triples for the stated relation/premise-extension properties. There are 81 entailment pairs. Sixteen standard equivalence patterns are assessed on eight three-atom valuations. Cases distinguish valid inference from a true individual conditional, complete from restricted valuation search, and inconsistent from empty premises. Eight specified invalid evaluator inputs are rejected. A separate four-rule line checker accepts three selected paths and rejects five specified faulty paths; no subproofs, assumption discharge or completeness proof are supplied. Six files: PDF, TXT, definitions JSON, references JSON, original Python and computed results. The same assistant repeated the standalone run and obtained identical result bytes; shared errors remain possible. Neither algorithm comparison nor repeat execution is independent external validation. No free-text parser, first-order logic, complete natural deduction, empirical premise truth or causal effects tested. The conservative comparison with 3,236 preceding published entries consolidates 126 formulations and leaves 74 additional editorial cores; typed dual-law families preserve distinct rules, not unrestricted synonym identity. Source reading is selective, with exact forall x: Calgary HTML revision c5cb415 dated 2026-09-27 and bounded sections stated; no source pages, individual application stories, table images, exercise solutions or code redistributed. Own prior works are not independent confirmation. CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 covers only available rights in this edition; source CC BY 4.0 rights and embedded font rights remain intact. No professional legal or independent translation review. DOI provides archival identity, not peer review or immunity from criticism.

title: AI-Driven Multi-Dimensional Course Assessment and SHS Strand Recommendation System
abstract: Senior High School (SHS) students often face challenges in selecting the most appropriate academic strand due to limited assessment tools and the continued reliance on traditional guidance practices. These methods frequently lack objectivity and comprehensive evaluation, resulting in mismatches between students’ competencies, interests, and their chosen academic pathways. Such misalignment may affect students’ academic performance, educational direction, and future career readiness. This study aimed to develop an AI-Driven Multi-Dimensional Course Assessment and SHS Strand Recommendation System designed to objectively evaluate student competencies and generate strand recommendations that align with learners’ abilities, interests, and career potential. The system intends to support students, teachers, and guidance personnel by providing data-driven insights that can assist in making informed academic decisions. The research employed a quantitative–descriptive design integrated with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). The system was developed using an Input–Process–Output (IPO) conceptual framework combined with Agile Software Development Methodology, enabling iterative system improvement and structured data processing. The platform utilizes a 30-dimension assessment model measuring cognitive skills, literacy and communication abilities, technical aptitude, and personality-interest indicators. Student responses are processed through a structured scoring model and analyzed using an AI-powered evaluation module to generate strand recommendations, competency profiles, and career-related insights, which are presented in a downloadable evaluation report. The results are presented in a comprehensive evaluation report that users can download and use for academic guidance and decision-making. Evaluation results showed strong system performance and user acceptance. Based on the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model, IT experts gave the system an overall mean score of 3.95, indicating a high level of software quality and functionality. System users rated the platform with an overall mean score of 4.00, interpreted as Highly Acceptable, reflecting positive user experience and effectiveness. This finding clearly demonstrates that the system can provide data-driven guidance in SHS strand selection, reduce academic-career mismatches, and support better educational alignment and long-term career readiness among students.

title: Histopatoloji görüntülerinde anlamsal çekirdek segmentasyonu için ön işleme tekniklerinin karşılaştırmalı analizi
abstract: Histopatolojik çekirdek segmentasyonu, bilgisayar destekli patoloji uygulamalarında temel bir bileşen olmakla birlikte, boyama protokolleri, tarayıcı farklılıkları ve doku hazırlama süreçlerinden kaynaklanan varyasyonlar, derin öğrenme tabanlı modellerin genellenebilirliğini olumsuz etkileyebilmektedir. Bu çalışmada, MoNuSeg veri seti üzerinde SegFormer-B2 mimarisi kullanılarak, yaygın önişleme bileşenlerinin anlamsal çekirdek segmentasyonu performansı üzerindeki etkisi kontrollü bir deneysel çerçevede incelenmiştir. Tüm deneylerde model mimarisi ve eğitim prosedürü sabit tutulmuş, yalnızca önişleme adımları değiştirilmiştir; bu sayede önişleme bileşenlerinin göreli katkıları kontrollü ve yorumlanabilir biçimde analiz edilmiştir. Bu kapsamda, boyama normalizasyonu (Macenko), kontrast iyileştirme (CLAHE), uzamsal filtreleme (Gauss) ve renk tabanlı veri artırmanın tekil ve birleşik kullanımlarını içeren K0–K7 önişleme konfigürasyonları karşılaştırmalı olarak değerlendirilmiştir. Model performansı, bölge tabanlı örtüşmeyi değerlendiren Dice ve IoU ile sınır duyarlılığını yansıtan BF1 ve HD95 ölçütleri kullanılarak raporlanmıştır. Elde edilen sonuçlar, önişleme adımlarının segmentasyon performansı üzerinde konfigürasyona ve bileşen etkileşimlerine duyarlı olduğunu göstermektedir. Gauss tabanlı uzamsal filtreleme, tüm ölçütlerde dengeli iyileşmeler sağlayarak sınır kararlılığını desteklemiştir. Renk tabanlı veri artırma bölge tabanlı ölçütlerde sınırlı fakat istikrarlı kazanımlar üretirken, CLAHE ve Macenko temelli normalizasyonların belirli konfigürasyonlarda performans düşüşlerine yol açabildiği gözlenmiştir. Bu bulgular, önişleme tasarımının kritik bir değişken olduğunu ve daha fazla önişlemenin her zaman daha iyi segmentasyon performansı anlamına gelmediğini ortaya koymaktadır.

title: Modus Ponens in the logic of reasons
abstract: This paper addresses the question whether Modus Ponens holds in the logic of reasons, that is, whether a binary connective that formally represents the relation ‘is a reason for’ should validate Modus Ponens. As will emerge, there is no straightforward answer to this question, since different intuitions about reasons pull in different directions. Our aim is to show how these intuitions can be captured within a single formal framework.

title: Exploring the moderating effects of flow experience in strengthening artificial intelligence-based customer interactions on social commerce
abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the effect of utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) in social commerce on increasing consumer engagement, specifically in terms of engagement and conversion rates. It also examines the role of flow experience in strengthening this relationship. Design/methodology/approach This study collected data from 354 Indonesian social commerce shoppers. Covariance based Structural Equation Modeling was employed to analyze the data following the two-stage procedure. First, the measurement model was assessed for validity and reliability. Second, the structural hypothesis model was evaluated to test the proposed hypotheses. Findings The utilization of AI significantly influences social commerce visitor interactions in terms of engagement and conversion. Both variables can enhance customer satisfaction, thereby impacting repurchase intention. Flow experience also strengthens the relationship between engagement and satisfaction, offering practical guidance for creating immersive and enjoyable user experiences. Originality/value This study extends the existing social commerce and AI literature by positioning flow experience as a moderator, explaining how and when engagement and conversion translate into satisfaction. Unlike previous models that primarily focus on direct effects, this research introduces psychological mechanisms that capture the conditional and experiential nature of AI-driven interactions, thereby offering a more comprehensive understanding of consumer behavior in social commerce.

title: MolLean: A Process-Verifiable Language for Chemical Reasoning
abstract: Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state. A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. Meanwhile, a typed witness protocol separates native structural checks from externally supplied measurements. We further introduce MolLean-MCP, a stateful tool interface that exposes these transitions, checks, and readouts during generation: the model receives feedback to decide its next action, and rejected actions leave the state unchanged. MolLean supports one-pass trace execution, whole-trace refinement, and interactive reasoning through MolLean-MCP. We evaluate these three modes with direct chain-of-thought on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks spanning molecular generation, editing, optimization, and reactions. With Qwen3.6-27B, whole-trace refinement outperforms direct chain-of-thought on all 12 tasks. MolLean-MCP complements whole-trace refinement with stepwise verification feedback, reaching better performance in reaction tasks. Together, these results highlight an executable foundation for chemical reasoning, in which explicit chemical commitments can be checked and revised rather than remaining solely in free-form explanations.

title: HGRP: Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network for Routability Prediction
abstract: Routability prediction enables rapid evaluation of placement quality without routing, providing effective feedback for routability-driven placement optimization. Recent machine learning methods have achieved efficient routability prediction through data-driven approach. However, their prediction performance highly depends on the capability of input representations to capture essential circuit information. To address the limitations of existing circuit representations in simultaneously preserving logical topology, physical layout and routing resource information, this paper proposes HGRP, a heterogeneous graph neural network for routability prediction. HGRP models the cells, nets, and routing grids as distinct types of nodes and explicitly represents topological connectivity, spatial mapping, and grid adjacency, thereby constructing a heterogeneous graph representation that preserves multi-level circuit semantics. Based on the representation, a heterogeneous message passing mechanism is developed to enable information interaction and feature fusion among distinct types of nodes, effectively learning the complex correlations between circuit structures and routing behaviors. Experimental results on the CircuitNet dataset show that HGRP improves F1-score by 18.69\% relative improvements compared with the state-of-the-art in the congestion prediction task. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ShenShan123/HGPR.

title: Beyond Benchmark Accuracy: A Diagnostic Test for LLM Chemical Prediction
abstract: LLMs have achieved strong performance on chemical prediction benchmarks. However, existing evaluation methods typically provide target entity identity information directly, making it difficult to determine whether model predictions arise from transferable structure-property reasoning capabilities or rely on target-related contextual information or memory retrieval. We propose the Identity-Blinded Reasoning Diagnostic framework to evaluate chemical prediction models when target entity identity information is hidden. In this framework, the target is no longer directly defined by its entity identity, but instead by a known source entity and an explicit structural edit operation. This setting preserves the information required to determine the target while reducing the opportunity for models to access target identity cues. We evaluate this framework across six tasks spanning odor prediction, molecular property prediction, retrosynthesis, and reaction yield prediction. The results show that models generally achieve better prediction performance when source and target entity properties are consistent. Providing explicit source entity labels further strengthens this dependence. Moreover, while keeping the target entity, structural change, and ground-truth label unchanged, replacing only the source entity label causes some model predictions to systematically shift toward the substituted source labels. These results indicate that high benchmark accuracy in chemical prediction tasks does not necessarily imply that LLMs possess reliable structure-property reasoning capabilities. Our diagnostic framework provides a controlled evaluation approach for testing whether models can genuinely update predictions according to entity changes. The framework can be extended to other AI for Science tasks, particularly those where targets can be defined through transformations of known entities.

title: Long-Prompt Zero-Shot TTS: Benchmarking Prosody Reproduction Beyond Voice Cloning
abstract: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) typically conditions on a short speech prompt, which conveys timbre but provides only limited evidence of a speaker's prosodic patterns. We formulate Long-Prompt Zero-Shot TTS, a task that uses long speech prompts at inference time to reproduce speaker-specific prosody without target-speaker fine-tuning. We introduce LP-TTS-Bench, a bilingual benchmark of 37 speakers with 63.95 prompt hours and 2,728 held-out test utterances. Beyond intelligibility and timbre similarity, LP-TTS-Bench evaluates timing, prominence, intonation, and model-based prosody metrics, enabling multidimensional evaluation of prosody reproduction. As a reference system, we develop LPTTS, whose hierarchical Long-Prompt Encoder compresses long speech prompts into a fixed number of continuous prosody vectors. Experiments show improvements in several prosodic dimensions over a short-prompt baseline, with overall gains as prompt duration increases up to approximately 10 minutes and saturation at longer durations.

title: Runtime Monitoring of Supermartingale Certificates
abstract: Supermartingale certificates formally guarantee temporal properties of discrete and continuous-time stochastic dynamical systems. However, these guarantees rely on a mathematical model of the world, leaving a sim-to-real gap that can invalidate them for the deployed system. We formulate the runtime monitoring problem for supermartingale certificates, in which a monitor observes a single system trajectory and raises an alarm when there is sufficient statistical evidence that the supermartingale certificate has been violated during execution. We present an algorithm to automatically construct a monitor using betting-based sequential tests that bound the probability of ever raising a false alarm at a user-specified level. Within this betting framework, we formulate strategies that allow the monitor to exploit spatial regularity to improve detection power while preserving this statistical guarantee. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on supermartingale certificate benchmarks from the literature.

title: F2A-ObjectNav: An Adaptive Agentic Architecture for Object-Goal Navigation
abstract: Object-goal navigation requires an embodied agent to explore an unfamiliar environment, identify a target object, navigate toward candidate instances, and reliably determine whether the observed object satisfies the mission goal. This work investigates this problem through a two-stage development process. In Stage I, a fixed modular framework is used to examine combinations of exploration, object detection, and target validation methods. The results reveal clear trade-offs among navigation performance, validation reliability, execution time, and model-related cost, with no single fixed configuration remaining preferable across all evaluated conditions. These observations motivate F2A-ObjectNav (Fixed-to-Adaptive Object-Goal Navigation), an adaptive agentic architecture in which a rule-based Supervisor coordinates specialized components for navigation and exploration, object detection, target validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory. The architecture uses event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional semantic guidance while retaining lightweight execution during normal operation. F2A-ObjectNav is evaluated over 25 episodes in each of AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, achieving success rate (SR) / success-weighted path length (SPL) values of 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37, respectively. In addition to task-level metrics, architecture-specific behavioral metrics are used to characterize semantic-guidance usage, strategy switching, recovery activation, memory-supported behavior, and decision stability. The results show different patterns of adaptive intervention across the three environments, with higher intervention frequencies observed in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR than in AI2-THOR.

title: Robust Because Coarse, or Robust Because Planned? A Research Agenda for Training-Data Provenance After the Aggregate-Disclosure Turn, in Which Granularity Buys Statistical Power, Prior Randomisation Buys Soundness, and Per-Example Value Has Neither
abstract: Life of Research (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Regulators have chosen coarse disclosure of training data: the template for the EU AI Act's public summary of training content asks for lists of large datasets, a summary of the most relevant crawled domains and a description of how opt-outs were honoured, and does not require a list of individual works. Compensation schemes, opt-out enforcement and licensing markets, by contrast, need a debt from a model to a particular work, and the technical literature reports that per-example attribution is unstable across training runs and can be manipulated. The natural reading is that provenance is robust where it is coarse and gameable where it pays. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that granularity is not the variable that separates the robust claims from the gameable ones. The paper separates four quantities that travel under the word provenance - composition, inclusion, exposure and contribution - and three parties who may be adversarial - the developer, the contributor and the valuator. Aggregation raises statistical power: membership inference that is at chance for single sentences reaches an AUROC of 0.943 on 500-document collections, and influence estimates for groups track actual group effects with rank correlations of 0.8 to 1.0 in convex models. Power is not soundness. A post-hoc test cannot sample its own null hypothesis at any granularity, while a randomised mark inserted before release gives a bounded false-positive rate for a single rightsholder. Coarse units leak: filtering a corpus by current robots.txt opt-outs cut the share of documents matching New York Times text only from 0.354 to 0.267 percent, much of the remainder being copies republished elsewhere. Per-example contribution is the one quantity that is unstable, gameable by contributors, who raised their compensation share to between 185 and 644 percent of its unperturbed value, and gameable by valuators who choose the utility. The paper consolidates the measured values in a table, maps six obligations to the quantity each needs, gives a decision procedure for choosing an instrument, and names seven measurements that would settle what the published record leaves open.

Per-example contribution is the one quantity that is unstable, gameable by contributors, who raised their compensation share to between 185 and 644 percent of its unperturbed value, and gameable by valuators who choose the utility. The paper consolidates the measured values in a table, maps six obligations to the quantity each needs, gives a decision procedure for choosing an instrument, and names seven measurements that would settle what the published record leaves open.

title: AFAI: Code, agent study and results for "Asymmetric Federated Agentic Intelligence"
authors: Gustav Olaf Yunus Laitinen-Fredriksson Lundstrom Imanov
abstract: Code, agent study and results accompanying the paper "Asymmetric Federated Agentic Intelligence" by Olaf Yunus Laitinen Imanov, Rana Irem Turhan and Isgandar Jafarli (equal contribution), NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agentic AI Benchmarks and Applications for Enterprise Tasks (AABA4ET). The paper formalizes Asymmetric Federated Agentic Intelligence (AFAI), in which institutional agents that differ in model, tools, privacy budget and decision rights collaborate by releasing differentially private counts over a public vocabulary of plan templates instead of parameters or free text. This record contains:- the controlled simulation of a six-node anti-money-laundering federation (Fin-Syndicate), in Python and NumPy only. Running "python afai_sim.py" writes results/results.json, from which the tables of the paper are generated; a rerun with Python 3.11 and NumPy 2.4 reproduces the archived file byte for byte;- the real-agent study with 12 open-weight language models from five families (0.8B to 27B parameters): code, prompts, plan templates, synthetic data generators, all logged model outputs and the federation replay, which can be recomputed on a CPU from the released records;- the analysis scripts that generate every table and every number quoted in the paper from the released result files;- the paper (PDF). The agent study was run on NVIDIA GH200 GPUs of the Roihu supercomputer, CSC - IT Center for Science, Finland.

title: BanglaTrace: A Cross-Stage Benchmark Tracing Text Normalization Errors from Text to Speech.
abstract: This dataset is a cross-stage benchmark for the front end of Bangla text-to-speech. It follows the outputs of text normalization (TN) through grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) conversion and speech synthesis, so that errors can be located and measured at each stage. It contains 485 author-written Bangla sentences in 40 categories (numbers, dates and times, money and measurements, acronyms, code-mixed and romanized text, identifiers, and plain-text controls) across 12 application domains. The sentences have 548 annotated non-standard-word spans and 2,181 accepted sentence readings at three levels (PRIMARY, STRICT, FULL), and are split into 93 development and 392 test sentences. The record also includes: saved outputs of six TN conditions: raw text, bnNumerizer, NumericContext, PyBangla, Google's public WFST grammars, and an adapted Kingfisher with GPT-OSS 120B; TN-to-G2P interface results for Epitran and eSpeak NG; speech results for two synthesizers with different input representations, the character-input MMS-TTS and the subword-input Indic Parler-TTS, each recognized by MMS-ASR and Whisper large-v3; error-source and failure-type analyses; G2P agreement with the Google Bengali pronunciation lexicon; the systematic-review appraisal records; the code that regenerates every table and figure. It accompanies the article "Tracing Errors from Text to Speech: A Systematic Review and Cross-Stage Benchmark of Bangla Text Normalization and Pronunciation" (submitted to ACM TALLIP). Data and results are released under CC BY 4.0 and code under the MIT License; see README.md inside the archive.

title: Joint Optimization of Retrieval-Augmented KV Caching and Adaptive Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Generation
abstract: Abstract Retrieval-assisted key–value (KV) reuse and speculative decoding remove different costs, but their naive composition can leave draft and verification overhead after prefill is shortened. RAKV-ASD combines exact causal prefix validation with a measured controller that selects reuse and k∈{0,1,2,4,6,8}. Across 3,600 timed executions on two GPT-2-family pairs, every greedy output matched target-only decoding. Pooled results show 64.0% lower latency and 170.8% higher throughput than reuse plus fixed k=4, while remaining within 0.45% of the KV-only baseline. The controller selected k=0, achieved 100% k-decision accuracy and 0.32% mean regret despite 32.1% point-prediction MAPE because costs rank actions rather than provide calibrated latency forecasts. Sensitivity and a third-pair study place the nonzero-k crossover at predicted acceptance ≥0.894. The result is a measured boundary and a mechanism that avoids counterproductive speculation, not a universal speedup.

title: Speech Technology for Nigerian Languages in Safety-Critical Voice Applications: A Systematic Mapping Study of Datasets, Models, and Telephony Readiness
abstract: This registration defines a systematic mapping study conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines to investigate the acoustic and operational readiness of speech technologies for safety-critical maternal health triage. The study will map existing datasets and speech technology models—including automatic speech recognition (ASR), text-to-speech (TTS), language identification, and code-switching detection—for Yorùbá, Igbo, Hausa, Nigerian Pidgin, and Nigerian-accented English. The primary objective is to characterize the distribution, coverage, and maturity of existing resources and to identify substantive gaps and voids in the literature. Particular attention will be given to the critical distinction between benchmark performance obtained on clean, studio-quality speech and operational robustness under realistic 8 kHz telephony compression, which is highly relevant to telephone-based or low-bandwidth maternal health triage. Where the systematic search identifies a consistent absence of evidence concerning the pronunciation, recognition, or synthesis of medical and clinical vocabulary in Nigerian languages, this absence will be recorded and analysed as an evidence gap. Such findings will not be attributed solely to limitations of the search strategy or interpreted merely as methodological limitations. Instead, persistent absence across the identified evidence base will be treated as a substantive finding concerning the current state and coverage of speech-technology resources for these languages.

title: Python and OOP
abstract: This chapter provides a comprehensive introduction to object-oriented programming (OOP) in Python, focusing on creating and managing custom classes. It begins by explaining Python’s accessibility conventions, noting that while everything in Python is public, conventions like single underscore (_) for protected and double underscore (__) for private variables and methods are used, though not strictly enforced. This chapter introduces three ways to define a class (e.g., class MyClass, class MyClass(), class MyClass(object)), emphasizing that all Python 3 classes implicitly inherit from the object class. Key concepts like instance variables (unique to each object) versus class variables (shared across instances) are illustrated with examples like the Company class. This chapter also covers magic methods (e.g., __init__, __str__, __repr__), which enable custom behavior for object initialization, string representation, and comparisons, as shown in code snippets like MyPoint3D.py and ComparePoint3D.py. This chapter then provides examples of custom Python iterable classes, such as the Cube class, which implements __iter__ and __next__ for iteration, and highlights errors in invalid iterator definitions (e.g., WrongIter.py). It explores advanced OOP concepts like encapsulation, demonstrated in encapsulation1.py, where private methods handle internal logic, and inheritance, both single (e.g., SingleInherit1.py) and multiple (e.g., MultipleInherit1.py). Polymorphism is explained through examples like Polymorphism1.py, showcasing how methods can operate on different class instances via duck-typing. Practical applications include managing collections of objects, such as in the Employees class, and data structures like linked lists (LLAndList.py, LLAndDict.py) and priority queues (PriorityQueue.py), which use custom classes to organize data efficiently. This chapter also addresses advanced topics like abstract base classes (via the abc module) for enforcing method implementation and the use of inspect for examining class hierarchies (e.g., display_base_classes.py). It contrasts Python’s flexible OOP approach with stricter languages like Java, noting features like virtual methods and the absence of interfaces. This chapter concludes with a summary reinforcing these concepts, encouraging further exploration of OOP for robust Python programming. Each code example, such as FoodPreferences.py for inheritance and Counter1.py for iterators, provides practical demonstrations of these principles, making this chapter a solid foundation for understanding Python’s OOP capabilities.

title: What and Where in Identifying and Quantifying Conventions in Humans and AI Agents
abstract: Cooperative success rests in part on implicit communication. Partners converge on conventions: regularities that give an action meaning beyond its direct effect. Yet conventions are usually observed only indirectly: a score drop when partners are swapped shows that a convention existed, but not what it was or where it was used. In the card game Hanabi, the exact probability that a play fails can be computed from the hints received and the cards in view. Players who use conventions succeed more often than this prediction allows; the resulting margin is the convention gap. Off-belief learning provides a hierarchy of agents (levels 1-5) whose first level uses no conventions by construction and whose later levels use progressively more. For humans and these agents on one scale, we ask what the conventions are and where they are used. On what: in two independently collected corpora of human games, humans show a larger gap than every agent level. On the conventions both populations use, however, humans do no better than level 2. The human advantage is concentrated in a situation that no agent level learns to use: hints that point to a card other than the ones they touch. On where: conventions depend on what the player already knows about the card, not on how recently it was hinted, and they are used most in the mid-game; humans use them earlier and later in the game than the agents. In interventions on the agents, blocking a single high-gap situation costs little, because meaning reroutes to other situations, but blocking several together costs far more than the sum of the single costs. Thus, the convention gap turns conventions from an inferred cause of score loss into a measurable, comparable, and causally testable object.

title: Multimodal Medical Image Parsing with Task-Specific Low-Rank Adapters
abstract: Adapting a single vision-language model to medical image parsing requires training choices that reflect the demands of each task. We study task-specific adaptation with Qwen3.5-9B for FLARE 2026 Task 3, covering six task families and seven imaging modalities. Our system couples a shared, frozen 4-bit backbone with LoRA adapters selected from the input question. We customize adapter ranks and prompts, rebalance rare classification targets, and supplement regression training with dermatology classification examples. On the fixed internal holdout, the task-specific adapters achieve a dataset-macro balanced accuracy of 0.7791 for classification, a dataset-macro micro-F1 of 0.6286 for multi-label classification, a counting mean absolute error (MAE) of 11.73, a dataset-macro detection F1 of 0.8914, a dataset-macro regression MAE of 9.78, and a report-generation CRIMSON score of 0.8204. On the organizer's 1,703-example hidden-validation set, the submitted system achieves 0.8496 classification balanced accuracy, 0.5338 sample-averaged multi-label F1, and 14.5950 regression MAE. The final 30.1 GB container averages 3.1 seconds per case, including model loading, and produces identical outputs across repeated verification runs. The benefits vary across tasks, supporting the use of task-specific adapter configurations and image budgets within a shared medical vision-language model. Code is available at https://github.com/TahaSabir0/FLARE26-Hexapus.

title: Who Speaks When the Chatbot Answers? Generative AI as Institutional Speech
abstract: When a branded chatbot answers a customer, the reply is often taken as the institution speaking. This paper treats that uptake as a media and communication problem rather than as a model-accuracy problem alone. Using Erving Goffman’s account of footing—the gap between who animates an utterance and who stands as its principal—and Austin and Searle’s account of commitments as speech acts, we read the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal decision in Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024 BCCRT 149) as a public episode of institutional speech gone wrong. A website chatbot told Jake Moffatt that a bereavement fare could be claimed retroactively within ninety days; a different page on the same site, and later human staff, denied that path. Air Canada argued it should not be held liable for the chatbot; the tribunal disagreed and ordered damages. The case lets us follow authorization, utterance, uptake, contested repair, and the failed attempt to split the animator from the principal. While systematic reviews of AI disadvantages map privacy, displacement, and bias at a macroeconomic scale, they leave open this micro-communicative surface where an institution’s name is attached to a fluent reply. We argue that handoff to a named human is part of the speech act when commitment is at stake, not an optional engineering fallback. References [1] J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words. title: Software repository for transfer learning for photovoltaic forecasting under data scarcity
abstract: This repository provides the software and configuration files accompanying the manuscript "Transfer Learning for Photovoltaic Forecasting under Data Scarcity: Technical and Economic Value of Generic Multi-System Pretraining under Domain Shift". The codebase implements the complete computational workflow for reproducing the study, including PV and meteorological data processing, generic multi-system model pretraining, target-only forecasting, transfer learning, and physical PV modeling. It further includes scripts for operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) data collection, cold-start model evaluation, day-ahead PV–battery dispatch optimization, and economic assessment using imbalance settlement. The repository contains Python source code, configuration files, supporting services, and documentation of the processing and evaluation workflows. Large input datasets and intermediate files are not fully included and must be reconstructed separately. This archive is intended to support transparency, reproducibility, and further methodological development rather than to present the experimental results.

title: THE ROLE OF SYNTACTIC ANALYSIS IN NATURAL LANGUAGE PROCESSING AND COMPUTER LINGUISTICS
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and digital communication has significantly increased the importance of technologies capable of processing human language. Every day, large volumes of textual information are generated through websites, scientific publications, social networks, digital libraries, and electronic communication platforms. Analyzing this information efficiently requires computational methods that can identify not only individual words but also the grammatical relationships that connect them. abstract: FINDING: Quantum teleportation advances in 2025–2026 center on logical gate teleportation (Oxford) and single-photon interference confirmation (MIT), with no new fundamental constants or ratios reported. | MATH: No new equations; relies on existing formalism — Bell-state measurement, entanglement fidelity \(F = \langle\psi|\rho|\psi\rangle\), and teleportation protocol \(|\psi\rangle \to |\psi\rangle\) via shared Bell pair \(|\Phi^+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle + |11\rangle)\). title: Uni (Universal Neural Interaction / Universal Node Identity)
abstract: Traditional document and serialization formats (PDF, DOCX, HTML, JSON) are designed for human visual rendering or verbose text parsing, forcing AI systems and edge processors to waste computational resources translating character streams into multidimensional vectors. The **`.uni`** standard eliminates this bottleneck by operating as a binary-serialized, non-executable semantic and telemetry container engineered for direct tensor operations, granular cryptographic disclosure, and automated cryptographic notarization.

title: MARS - A foundational map auto-regressor
abstract: Map generation tasks feature extensive non-structural vectorized data (e.g., points, polylines, and polygons) and thus pose significant challenges to common pixel-wise generative models. Conventional approaches use multiple stages, first segmenting these features at the pixel level and then performing vectorized post-processing, with errors and complexity compounding at each stage. Motivated by the recent success of auto-regressive language modeling, we propose the first map foundation model, named Map Auto-Regressor (MARS), that is capable of generating both multi-polyline road networks and polygon buildings in a unified manner. For training MARS, we collected to our knowledge the largest multi-class map extraction dataset totaling 3.4M examples, which we call MAP-3M. Across four road and building datasets, MARS outperforms or matches the performance of multistage baselines. Additionally, we develop a "Chat with MARS" capability that enables interactive human-in-the-loop map generation and correction, supported by the auto-regressive nature of our end-to-end approach. We release our MAP-3M dataset and project demo page at (1) https://huggingface.co/datasets/bag-lab/MAP-3M and (2) https://huggingface.co/spaces/bag-lab/MARS, respectively.

title: Investigating Behavior Cloning from Few Demonstrations for Autonomous Driving based on Bird's-Eye View in Simulated Cities
abstract: This paper investigates the use of Behavior Cloning (BC) for autonomous driving from a bird's-eye view (BEV) perspective in simulated urban environments. BC uses supervised learning to mimic expert driving behaviors. Previous works have applied BC in the CARLA simulator but did not fully address the challenges of traffic light compliance. Our approach enhances BC by integrating a kernel density estimator to adjust training sample weights based on action density, thereby improving the learning of rare but critical actions such as stopping at red lights and accelerating at green lights, specially in scenarios of scarce number of expert demonstrations. Using BEV inputs, which provide an abstract top-down view of the driving environment, our method simplifies the policy learning process. The trained convolutional neural network (CNN) outputs steering and acceleration actions based on these BEV inputs and additional state variables. Experimental results in the CARLA simulator demonstrate that our weighted BC method significantly improves driving performance, achieving higher route completion compared to standard BC. This weighted approach proved to be crucial in learning correct driving behaviors, particularly in test environments not encountered during training, highlighting its potential for enhancing autonomous vehicle navigation.

title: How GUI Agents Fail: GraceBench for Execution Stability Diagnosis
abstract: As GUI agents are increasingly deployed for mobile task automation, their reliability depends not only on final task outcomes, but also on whether they reach these outcomes through stable interaction trajectories. In automation workflows, unnecessary actions, detours, and execution errors can add noise to collected data, introduce irreversible side effects, or undermine trust, even when the agent eventually completes the task. It is therefore important to systematically diagnose the execution stability, including whether an agent deviates from a feasible path, enters a loop, becomes stagnant, or recovers from unstable actions. Existing benchmarks, however, primarily assess final task success or a small set of intermediate milestones, leaving step-level execution behavior unclear. To bridge this gap, we introduce GraceBench, an online evaluation framework that represents the reachable interaction space of mobile applications as UI Transition Graphs (UTGs), providing a structural reference for step-level execution diagnosis. To support reliable alignment between dynamic UI observations and graph states, GraceBench uses video-grounded trajectory evaluation over this graph-aligned representation, assessing process stability beyond final success with metrics such as deviation rate, loop burden rate, and recovery ability. GraceBench contains 169 tasks spanning 10 applications and constructs 10 UTGs with 2,909 canonical GUI states and 3,116 observed transitions. Across 3,718 trajectories, GraceBench shows that outcome scores hide execution instability: GPT-5.6 Sol achieves the highest success rate (SR) but the lowest recovery ability, 51.24% of successful runs still contain a deviation or loop, and trajectories with the same success rate (SR) and completion rate (CR) can differ substantially in recovery behavior. Code and data will be released on https://iaie-physicalai.github.io/GraceBench.

title: RepostAI: A Multilingual AI-Powered Content Repurposing Platform for Cross-Platform Social Media Publishing in English, Tamil and Thanglish
abstract: Authors who publish for Tamil-speaking audiences routinely rewrite one message for LinkedIn, X (Twitter), Instagram, WhatsApp and e-mail, and must also choose between formal Tamil and the romanised Tamil–English mixture widely used online, commonly called Thanglish. This paper presents RepostAI, a lightweight web framework that converts a single piece of user content into fifteen platform- and language-specific drafts (five platforms in three language styles) through one request. The system accepts the source text, a content type and a tone; builds a constrained prompt that specifies the structure and length of each platform's output; sends the prompt to the Llama 3.3 70B model through the Groq inference API; repairs and parses the structured JSON reply; and presents the drafts in a language-switchable, copy-ready interface. The contribution is an integrated and inspectable pipeline, not a new language model: no model is trained or fine-tuned. The paper describes the architecture, the prompt-constraint specification, the response-handling method, the implementation and an evaluation methodology based on programmatically verifiable constraint compliance and native-speaker rating. The paper is explicit about maturity: Tamil and Thanglish quality have not yet been quantitatively evaluated, the model's published language-support list does not include Tamil, and no accuracy, latency or user-adoption figures are claimed. RepostAI is therefore presented as a working prototype and a foundation for later empirical study

title: Free Directions and Effective Learning: A Quotient-Space Reading of Neural Network Training
abstract: The parameter space of a neural network contains a large subspace of directions that do not change the function computed. Learning takes place on the quotient of the parameter space by this subspace. This note takes the quotient as the primary object and reads three standard facts of training—the degeneracy of the Fisher information, the composition of independent training signals, and the distinction between representability and trainability—as three aspects of one quotient-space structure. The reading is not new mathematics. It is an organizational choice: identification, estimability, and generalization become properties of a single geometric object, and questions about training dynamics become questions about the metric on the quotient. The framework is stated for feedforward networks with piecewise smooth activations and covers gauge freedom, kernel degeneracy, and distributed training under one language. One reading—the interpolation peak of double descent as a loss of uniform coercivity on the quotient—is not standard. Keywords: non-identifiable directions; gauge freedom; Fisher information; neural tangent kernel; double descent. MSC 2020: 68T07, 62H22, 15A63, 62F12.

title: Cost-Aware Adaptive Collaboration Dynamic Switching Between Independent Execution and Multi-LLM Cooperation
abstract: Multi-large language model (LLM) systems can improve problem-solving performance by combining models with complementary capabilities. However, collaboration introduces additional costs, including model invocation, communication, response aggregation, verification, and coordination latency. Activating multiple models for every task may therefore be inefficient, while relying exclusively on a single model may fail to exploit complementary expertise when collaboration is beneficial. This paper proposes Cost-Aware Adaptive Collaboration (CAAC), a framework that dynamically determines whether a task should be handled independently or collaboratively. The framework estimates the expected incremental utility of collaboration relative to independent execution, incorporating predicted answer quality, task uncertainty, model capability, inference cost, communication overhead, and latency constraints. A collaboration controller selects among independent execution, selective consultation, parallel collaboration, and escalation to additional models. The proposed decision policy can operate using historical performance estimates, task features, calibrated confidence signals, and online feedback. The framework also introduces a budget-constrained objective, a threshold-based switching policy, a contextual learning extension, and an evaluation protocol designed to measure both task quality and operational efficiency. Unlike approaches that prioritize answer quality alone, CAAC explicitly treats collaboration as a decision with measurable benefits and costs. The paper presents a conceptual and algorithmic framework rather than a claim of experimentally demonstrated superiority. Its effectiveness must be established through controlled comparisons across heterogeneous models, task categories, and cost settings.
