title: DISTRIBUTED QUANTUM NANO METROLOGY SWARMS AT THE LIMIT This high-density research monograph develops a falsifiable architecture for mobile and distributed quantum nano-probes that reconstruct temperature, strain, magnetic, electric, and defect-related fields during manufacturing. Its core tri-coupling is Heterogeneous Quantum Probes x Spatial Field Reconstruction x Independent References. Probe agreement is never treated as field truth: every qualified map must carry position and orientation covariance, cross-probe dependence, calibration ancestry, inverse-model priors, resolution kernels, and explicit unobservable regions. The governing comparison is deliberately severe. A quantum-hybrid constellation must outperform a high-precision central scan and a classical multiprobe array under matched acquisition time, energy, disturbance, bandwidth, cost, and reference quality. The minimum prototype uses known but blinded nano-field sources while injecting common calibration bias, position drift, probe dropout, and malicious offsets. The inversion is frozen before source labels are released, and measurement backaction is scored against the signal being reconstructed. The volume contains thirty diverse formula derivations, eighty-two chapters with five important research sections each, two hundred Research Gates, thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos, two hundred thirty-three unique Easter-Egg Equations, chapter-level DOI evidence anchors, and a clickable DOI evidence map. Its flagship embryo, the Quantum Probe Constellation, integrates heterogeneous sensitivity tensors, pose lineage, independent references, covariance-preserving inversion, blind validation, classical fallback, and successor reconstruction.

title: Complete information orders of quantum channels: equivalence and undecidability
abstract: About complete information orders of finite-dimensional quantum channels. With unrestricted finite quantum references, it claims equivalence of relative-entropy, Holevo, BKM, SLD Fisher-information and measured-chi-squared comparisons, with order reversal under genuine Stinespring complementation. It further claims coRE-completeness for strictly positive rational-complex POVMs, the absence of a computable sufficient SLD-reference cutoff, and inapproximability of a bounded additive entropy defect at every fixed positive additive accuracy. The companion manuscript is From complete channel order to capacity and one-way distillation; its capacity and distillation conclusions depend on the order results developed here.

title: Temporal Specification Guidance for Text-to-Video Generation
abstract: Text-to-video models often generate the visual concepts requested in natural language prompts but fail to satisfy their intended ordering, timing, and persistence requirements. We propose representing these requirements as specifications in a formal Temporal Logic, and introduce Temporal Specification Guidance (TSG), a training-free inference-time framework that turns temporal specifications into executable objectives for guiding video generation during sampling. TSG scores traces of visual concept evidence using differentiable quantitative semantics and uses the score's gradients to construct a specification-guided denoising direction. We instantiate this framework with video-text attention traces, efficient differentiable scores for Metric Temporal Logic, and gradient-derived attention biases. This instantiation requires neither an external concept classifier nor backpropagation through the video transformer. Its attention-steered forward pass yields a denoising direction that augments classifier-free guidance (CFG). On a benchmark of 220 prompts spanning 11 categories of temporal constraints, including ordered object entry and state transitions, this instantiation improves specification satisfaction accuracy over CFG by 9.5-20 percentage points across five models, with minimal memory overhead. These results demonstrate the potential of temporal specifications and differentiable satisfaction objectives as a flexible interface for controlling video generation.

title: Demonstration of a mobile ion-trap quantum device
abstract: Trapped-ion devices are being investigated for transportable applications, including the transfer of exotic charged particles between laboratories and the development of portable quantum technologies. To date, ion transport has been demonstrated only in magnetic (Penning) traps, whereas radiofrequency (Paul) traps are the predominant platform in quantum science. Here, we report the first transport of a few thousand ions confined in a linear Paul trap over distances of several kilometers, with transport durations of 15 and 45 min. These results establish a foundation for mobile trapped-ion quantum devices capable of operating while in motion and may enable the transport of exotic ions in Paul traps between experimental facilities.

title: Neural Wasserstein Splines: Representation-Invariant Second-Order Priors for Trajectory Inference
abstract: Population dynamics are often observed only as unpaired snapshots, which leave the evolution between measurements underdetermined. Second-order regularization can constrain it, but a penalty on the accelerations of sampled particles is a prior on joint particle paths, and different particle representations of the same marginal curve can have different acceleration costs. We therefore introduce Neural Wasserstein Splines (NWSP), a sample-based method that learns a continuous population curve under a Wasserstein smoothness prior. A neural network maps latent variables to the control points of a cubic spline in time, so samples at any time come from the spline basis without numerical integration. We project the generator's velocity onto gradients of a finite dictionary of scalar potentials and differentiate this measure-dependent projection in time, obtaining a finite-dimensional surrogate for the intrinsic Wasserstein acceleration, trained jointly with distributional fit losses. For a fixed dictionary and ridge parameter, we prove that the population penalty depends only on the marginal curve and bound its sensitivity to moment-estimation errors. Learned potentials (NWSP-N) sharpen acceleration estimates. On various synthetic and single-cell benchmarks, NWSP is highly competitive with transport and flow-based methods, ranking in the top two in 11 of 16 settings. The penalty improves on an unregularized spline in 13 of 16 settings and, while competitive with a particle-acceleration penalty, adds provable representation invariance.

title: Dependent Dirichlet processes via thinning
abstract: We introduce a novel framework to model a collection of samples using dependent Dirichlet processes constructed through a thinning mechanism. The proposed approach modifies the stick-breaking representation of the Dirichlet process by thinning, that is, setting equal to zero a random subset of the beta random variables used in the original construction. This results in a collection of dependent random distributions that exhibit both shared and unique atoms, with the shared ones assigned distinct weights in each distribution. The generality of the construction allows expressing a wide variety of dependence structures among the elements of the generated random vectors. Moreover, its simplicity facilitates the characterization of several theoretical properties and the derivation of efficient computational methods for posterior inference. A simulation study illustrates how a modeling approach based on the proposed process reduces uncertainty in group-specific inferences while preventing excessive borrowing of information when the data indicate it is unnecessary. This added flexibility improves the accuracy of posterior inference, outperforming related state-of-the-art models. An application to the Collaborative Perinatal Project data highlights the model’s capability to estimate group-specific densities and uncover a meaningful partition of the observations, both within and across samples, providing valuable insights into the underlying data structure.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Mechanisms and Mutual Mechanisms in General Intelligent Agents: A Parallel-World Framework for Dynamic Autonomous and Collaborative Intelligence
abstract: Intelligent agents can improve their behavior through autonomous internal processes, interactions with other agents, or combinations of both. However, systems that rely on a single operational mode may become constrained by repetitive strategies, limited perspectives, insufficient information exchange, or unnecessary coordination costs. This paper proposes the Parallel-World Adaptive Self–Mutual Intelligence Framework (PWASMI), a general conceptual and methodological framework for intelligent agents that adaptively switch between self-mechanisms and mutual mechanisms. Unlike approaches restricted to large language models, the proposed framework encompasses heterogeneous intelligent entities, including software agents, robotic agents, autonomous decision-making systems, adaptive controllers, and other computational or embodied forms of intelligence. The framework introduces parallel-world branching, in which multiple instances or developmental branches of the same originating agent pursue different strategies, hypotheses, objectives, or learning trajectories. These branches can operate independently, interact with one another, or collaborate with external agents that may have entirely different architectures and capabilities. A context-sensitive mechanism selector determines when to employ autonomous processing, intra-world interaction, inter-world collaboration, heterogeneous-agent collaboration, or hybrid configurations. The selection process considers estimated performance improvement, uncertainty, diversity, communication cost, computational cost, resource constraints, and historical outcomes. A formal problem formulation, architectural design, adaptive switching policy, algorithmic procedure, theoretical propositions, and experimental protocol are presented. The framework is intended to support dynamic intelligence coordination without requiring a fixed distinction between individual and collective operation. Its central hypothesis is that intelligent systems should determine not only what to do, but also whether the next step should be performed independently, collaboratively, or through interactions among divergent parallel worlds. The framework's effectiveness remains an empirical question to be investigated across heterogeneous environments and task families.

title: SCIENTIFIC AND METHODOLOGICAL FOUNDATIONS FOR IMPLEMENTING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TECHNOLOGIES IN THE CONTEXT OF DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION
abstract: This thesis examines the scientific and methodological foundations for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into organizational processes under digital transformation. Drawing on research in information systems, organizational AI readiness, software engineering, and risk management, it identifies the conditions under which AI adoption can generate measurable value. The analysis distinguishes technological deployment from organizational transformation and considers data governance, model selection, validation, human oversight, and continuous monitoring as interdependent implementation requirements. A conceptual, stage-based approach is proposed for connecting organizational objectives with technical design and operational performance. The contribution is methodological and analytical; no independent experimental outcomes or unverified performance improvements are claimed.

title: Deterministic Quantum Mechanics of Transformer In-Context Attention: Wavefunction Dirac-Delta Collapse via Optical-Mechanical Dual-Chassis
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) governed by softmax-based self-attention inherently suffer from non-deterministic token drift, attention dispersion, and cumulative hallucination. In this paper, we formalize in-context attention dynamics through a quantum mechanical perspective, modeling the attention distribution as a statistical probability density over the discrete token Hilbert space. To eliminate attention drift without model fine-tuning or external orchestration wrappers, we introduce an In-Context Virtual Machine (ICVM) operating via an Optical-Mechanical Dual-Chassis control system. The Optical Chassis partitions the softmax partition function into an immutable static core basis (collimated by 10 core persistent grounding assets) and a dynamic token basis, inducing a non-zero potential energy barrier that contracts the continuous probability wavepacket into a deterministic Dirac-delta function centered precisely at the target attractor state. Concurrently, the Mechanical Chassis executes direct POSIX kernel system calls (stat()) to enforce monotonic physical byte and line growth, halting the hardware tool bus whenever zero-tolerance engineering bounds are violated. Spanning extensive multi-turn empirical evaluations across complex reasoning domains, the dual-chassis system achieves a 0.00% hallucination rate, zero token drift, and O(1) state convergence with zero recurring cloud API overhead. This work provides an axiomatic mathematical proof and deterministic computing framework bridging theoretical attention thermodynamics and production-grade cybernetic autonomy. title: Attention-integrated hybrid CNN–vision transformer framework for robust multi-class cervical cytology classification using liquid-based cytology images
abstract: The grading of cervical cytology images is a challenging task because some morphological changes are subtle, there are class imbalances and variability in staining of lesion grades. In order to overcome such difficulties, this work suggests MAH-CerviT, a Multi-Scale Attention-Guided Hybrid Cervical Transformer framework that combines dense hierarchical convolutional learning and window-based contextual modeling. In contrast to the traditional convolutional networks that mainly learn the local texture patterns, or the transformer-based networks that only focus on the global attention mechanism to improve the model, MAH-CerviT is a synergistic network with three major components: (i) a multi-scale dense convolutional backbone to learn the hierarchical morphological feature aggregation, (ii) a sequential channel-spatial attention refinement module to selectively enhance the diagnostically relevant cellular regions, and (iii) a Swin Transformer encoder to model structured contextual dependency. The hybrid fusion approach allows to discriminate between morphologically similar classes like HSIL and LSIL in a balanced manner and keep the computational efficiency. Massive experiments in 5-fold stratified cross-validation show that MAH-CerviT has a total accuracy of 95.92, macro F 1-score of 95.52 and macro-AUC of 96.40, significantly higher than DenseNet-121, EfficientNet-B4, ViT-Base, and Swin Transformer baselines. It is statistically proved that the increase in comparison to the strongest baseline is significant (p < 0.01). Ablation experiments demonstrate that multi-scale aggregation, attention refinement and contextual encoding have a cumulative beneficial effect on the performance of the baseline convolutional model, which justifies the complementary role of each. The robustness analysis also shows that the performance remains stable even when there are image corruptions and less data. The suggested MAH-CerviT framework provides an efficient trade-off between the accuracy of the discrimination system and the computational efficiency, and it is a reliable and scalable tool to solve the automated cervical cancer screening application.

title: Continual Learning for Reliable In-Sequence Molecular Communication
abstract: This paper considers reliable in-sequence molecular communication, where bio-nanomachines exchange molecule-encoded information in a specified order, and investigates a new simulation-based method to incrementally evaluate communication protocols by gradually increasing the complexity of experimental settings. The proposed method, called Affine Memory Replay (AMR), builds a continual learning (CL) model to estimate communication performance between bio-nanomachines. AMR stores past simulation samples and synthesizes additional replay samples through interpolation and extrapolation between past samples. Through incremental performance estimation tasks, it replays both past and synthetic samples to regularize model updates, helping the model adapt to new experimental settings while retaining knowledge from earlier ones. Experimental results show that AMR significantly outperforms existing CL methods in maintaining overall estimation accuracy across sequentially learned estimation tasks. It effectively balances memory stability and learning plasticity under moderate training cost.

title: Remember, Revisit, Revise: Scaffold Memory for Long-Horizon 3D Geometry
abstract: Geometry foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D scene structure from video sequences, but maintaining consistent reconstructions over long horizons remains challenging. Feed-forward models process long sequences as independent, fixed-length frame windows and align their predictions, causing pose and reconstruction errors to accumulate across windows. Streaming models retain information from past frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when later observations reveal errors. To address this, we introduce Scaffold MemOry for Revision (SMORE), a framework equipping frozen geometry foundation models with a revisable external memory for long-horizon inference. Inspired by hippocampal associative memory in biological brains, which links spatial context with sensory experience, SMORE associates where an observer is with what it observes, enabling past observations to be stored, retrieved, verified against new evidence, and revised when inconsistencies are detected. We evaluate SMORE with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across all evaluated models, SMORE consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. By retaining corrected poses and observations, SMORE further improves the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. These results establish revisable external memory as a flexible interface for extending pretrained geometry models beyond fixed-context prediction toward iterative, error-correcting inference over long visual sequences.

title: Learning to Select Features with Manifold Deep Unfolding PCA
abstract: Unsupervised feature selection (UFS) is of great significance in image processing and pattern recognition. Nevertheless, existing model-based methods often rely on manually tuned hyperparameters, while deep learning-based methods generally require massive training data. To address these issues, this paper proposes an efficient manifold deep unfolding feature selection network (MDUFS-Net). Technically, we first incorporate the $\ell_{2,0}$-norm into the classic principal component analysis (PCA) framework, then unfold the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)-based iterative algorithm into an end-to-end trainable network, thereby enabling automatic parameter learning. Moreover, a manifold optimization strategy is developed to improve the numerical robustness. On this basis, we further extend MDUFS-Net into an enhanced variant called MDUFS-Net+ by introducing the $\ell_{0}$-norm for more discriminative feature representations. Extensive experiments validate that our proposed MDUFS-Net and MDUFS-Net+ outperform state-of-the-art methods in the UFS task, with promising performance in clustering. Our code is available at https://github.com/xianchaoxiu/MDUFS.

title: Answerability-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Helpdesk Question Answering: An Empirical Study of Similarity Thresholds and Grounding Strategies
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems can improve question answering by grounding large language model responses in external documents. However, enterprise deployments require not only relevant answers but also reliable abstention when the available knowledge base lacks sufficient evidence. This study investigates answerability control in an enterprise helpdesk RAG system by evaluating retrieval similarity thresholds, grounding instructions, and an explicit evidence-sufficiency mechanism. Experiments used a synthetic enterprise corpus containing 23 documents and 51 retrievable chunks. Five RAG configurations were compared on a 30-question development benchmark, and the selected configuration was evaluated on a separate 50-question test benchmark. The selected configuration achieved answerability precision, recall, and F1 scores of 1.00 on the test set, with no observed false refusals or unsupported answers. Retrieval recall at k was 0.9667, while automated keyword answer accuracy was 0.90. The findings indicate that similarity-threshold selection substantially influenced false refusals in the evaluated setting, while stronger grounding instructions improved keyword-match performance. However, the small synthetic corpus and benchmark limit the generalisability of these findings.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Parallel-World Self-Reflection and Mutual Reflection for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can improve their outputs through self-reflection, iterative refinement, and interaction with other models. However, self-reflection may repeatedly reproduce the same assumptions, while mutual reflection may introduce unnecessary communication costs, correlated errors, or misleading feedback. Existing approaches provide important foundations for self-refinement and multi-agent interaction, but a general framework that coordinates multiple reflection modes, including parallel-world self-reflection, adaptive mutual reflection among parallel instances, and cross-model reflection involving heterogeneous LLMs, remains an important research direction. This paper proposes Adaptive Parallel-World Reflection (APWR), a conceptual framework that dynamically switches between self-reflection and mutual reflection according to the evolving state of a reasoning process. In APWR, parallel worlds are defined as distinct reflection trajectories instantiated from the same underlying model but assigned different reflection objectives, perspectives, assumptions, or diagnostic priorities. Each trajectory initially reflects independently, preserving its own reasoning context and reducing premature convergence. When independent reflection becomes insufficient, selected trajectories exchange critiques and conduct mutual reflection. The framework can additionally incorporate heterogeneous LLMs that are not members of the original parallel-world group. A controller evaluates reflection progress, unresolved disagreements, estimated error risk, information diversity, and computational cost to select an appropriate reflection mode at each stage. Unlike a permanently independent or permanently collaborative strategy, APWR treats reflection mode selection as a sequential decision problem. The framework is designed to investigate whether adaptive coordination can improve reasoning accuracy, error detection, robustness, and computational efficiency. This paper formalizes the architecture, presents its operational procedure, defines evaluation metrics, and proposes an experimental protocol. Because the framework has not yet been empirically validated in this paper, its potential advantages are presented as testable hypotheses rather than established findings.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Correction and Mutual Correction for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently produce incorrect, incomplete, inconsistent, or unsupported outputs. Self-correction allows a model to inspect and revise its own output, whereas mutual correction enables multiple models to examine one another's outputs and propose revisions. However, relying exclusively on either mode may limit correction effectiveness. Self-correction may preserve the original model's mistaken assumptions, while mutual correction may introduce additional errors, encourage conformity, or incur unnecessary computational costs. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching between Self-Correction and Mutual Correction (ASSMC), a framework in which multiple LLMs dynamically switch between individual correction and cross-model correction according to the observed state of the correction process. Rather than requiring every model to follow a fixed correction strategy, ASSMC evaluates indicators such as unresolved errors, uncertainty, disagreement among models, correction history, and estimated correction effectiveness. It then selects the correction mode most appropriate to the current situation. Self-correction is preferred when a model can plausibly resolve an issue independently, whereas mutual correction is activated when persistent errors, substantial disagreement, or insufficient progress indicate a need for alternative perspectives. The system subsequently evaluates revised outputs and can switch modes again. The framework formalizes correction-mode selection as a sequential decision problem and introduces a proposed utility-based switching policy that considers quality improvement, computational cost, and the risk of introducing new errors. It also specifies an experimental methodology for comparing adaptive switching with fixed self-correction, fixed mutual correction, and other correction baselines. No empirical results are claimed in this conceptual study. The central research proposition is that dynamically coordinating the two correction modes may provide a more flexible balance between correction effectiveness, error diversity, and computational efficiency than using either mode exclusively.

title: Better Pedagogical Moves, Better Student Engagement? - An Evaluation of Pedagogical Strategies using AI Coaching Recommendations
abstract: This study uses a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness of recommending pedagogical strategies to tutors through an AI Coach platform for increasing student engagement in tutoring sessions. We will compare session-level measures of student engagement and tutor use of recommended pedagogical moves between the treatment and control groups to learn about the impact of recommending instructional practices to tutors on student engagement. Through this work, we expect to learn more about the potential for pedagogical moves that target relationship-building and math instruction to create a more engaging tutoring experience for students. Although existing evidence suggests that tutors who are experienced educators are associated with greater student learning gains than novice or inexperienced educators (Nickow et al., 2024), cost and recruitment considerations often lead tutoring providers to employ tutors who have little to no pedagogical experience and supplement pedagogical expertise with targeted training. Recent evidence shows that AI-powered coaching systems can increase educators' use of recommended pedagogical strategies, but only one other study we know of directly tests whether tutor use of specific pedagogical practices can improve student engagement or learning. In this study, we partnered with a tutoring provider to give a group of tutors access to Tutor Coach, an AI Coach platform, and randomized tutors into receiving weekly pedagogical strategy recommendations (treatment) or placebo recommendations (control) over a 12-week period. The pedagogical strategies recommended by TutorCoach included a combination of rapport-building and math instruction strategies, such as remembering to use the student's name and asking about student interests during the session, prompting the student to use the whiteboard to show their work, using worked examples to remediate math mistakes, and providing detailed praise and feedback. For each recommendation, the TutorCoach platform presented the strategy description and reasoning, and personalized examples generated from previous tutoring sessions led by the tutor. These examples were selected to show moments when the tutor used the strategy correctly in past sessions (when available), and moments when the tutor missed an opportunity to use the recommended strategy, followed by a suggestion for how to implement the strategy in that specific case. This study is designed to measure the impact of providing tutors with a curated set of recommendations of pedagogical strategies on tutor instructional moves and student engagement during tutoring sessions. We will use NLP methods to create measures of tutor moves that correspond to the moves recommended by TutorCoach from tutoring transcripts absent of tutor assignment information (blinded), and estimate the intent-to-treat effect of recommending pedagogical moves related to relationship-building and math instruction on tutor use of these moves and on the ratio of student talk time during sessions.

title: Integrated sentiment analysis of social media based on deep learning and topic modeling—a case study of Xiaomi's Weibo trending data
abstract: As social media serves as a public arena for information aggregation, the volume of user-generated comment data provides resources for corporate public opinion monitoring and product feedback. This paper proposes a sentiment analysis framework that integrates the BERT language model, jieba word segmentation and keyword extraction, and LDA topic modeling, and validates the approach using real-world Weibo comment data. Python web scraping was employed to collect user comments under Weibo trending topics related to Xiaomi from January 1 to March 20, 2025, yielding 12,396 valid samples after data cleaning. A random subset of 2,900 comments was manually annotated for fine-tuning the BERT model to perform three-class sentiment classification (positive, negative, neutral). Jieba segmentation and stop-word filtering were applied, TF-IDF statistics were computed, and LDA modeling was utilized to extract latent topics within positive and negative sentiment categories. The results indicate that the accuracy on the test set reaches 78.85%, confirming that the model exhibits stable classification performance and strong generalizability. BERT-based sentiment analysis reveals that positive sentiments account for the largest proportion. Keyword analysis and topic modeling indicate that positive comments center on "technological innovation" and "personal image"; negative comments concentrate on "product performance" and "brand service"; while neutral comments are factual descriptions of product specifications and event information. The study confirms that the proposed integrated approach effectively addresses the semantic complexity inherent in social media text sentiment analysis, offering an actionable solution for enterprise public opinion analysis in related domains.

title: Genuine multipartite entanglement measure based on G ω -concurrence
abstract: Abstract We introduce Gω-GME, a family of genuine multipartite entanglement measures defined via the geometric mean of a parameterized bipartite concurrence. We prove that Gω-GME satisfies all GME axioms, derive analytical expressions for GHZ and W states, and establish a strict entanglement hierarchy. Continuity under state perturbations is proven with explicit bounds. Compared with GMC, GqC, and GαC, Gω-GME resolves finer entanglement structures and offers greater flexibility through its extended parameter range. These features make Gω-GME a powerful and practical tool for multipartite entanglement quantification and quantum network certification.

title: Hyperspectral Characterization and Grade Discrimination of Metasedimentary Limestones
abstract: Diagnostic absorption spectroscopy across the Visible, Near-Infrared, and Shortwave Infrared (VNIR–SWIR: 0.4–2.5 µm) regimes enables rapid, non-destructive chemical and mineralogical characterization of lithological units. In this investigation, airborne imaging spectrometer data from AVIRIS-NG were integrated with laboratory-based spectroradiometric measurements to map and discriminate limestone sub-types within the metasedimentary sequences of the Kalinjara Formation, Aravalli Supergroup. By quantifying diagnostic absorption band parameters—specifically band depth (BD), wavelength position, and band asymmetry near 2.20–2.22 µm and 2.33–2.34 µm—we demonstrate that subtle spectral variations directly resolve intra-deposit purity and silica/alumina impurity distributions, providing an operational remote-sensing framework for high-precision deposit evaluation.

title: Inside the Language Model: A Primer on Transformers and Their Measurement for Psychologists
abstract: Psychologists who study language models increasingly meet results from inside the model: hidden states, layers, probes, lenses, patching. These results are usually written for readers trained in machine learning. This primer explains how a transformer language model is built and how its inner activity is measured, in plain language and with no mathematics beyond school level. Each concept is illustrated, where possible, with an example from our own studies of meaning reorganization. The aim: a reader trained in psychology can follow mechanistic work, judge what it can and cannot show, and enjoy it.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Parallel-World Self-Diagnosis and Mutual Diagnosis for Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate plausible but incorrect outputs, overlook their own reasoning errors, and reinforce initial mistakes during iterative refinement. Self-diagnosis enables a model to inspect its own outputs, whereas mutual diagnosis allows multiple model instances or different models to examine one another's outputs. However, relying exclusively on either mechanism may limit diagnostic diversity, increase computational costs, or preserve shared errors. This paper proposes a conceptual framework called Adaptive Parallel-World Diagnosis (APWD), which organizes multiple diagnostic branches derived from the same underlying model into parallel worlds with potentially different diagnostic objectives, hypotheses, and analytical strategies. The framework adaptively switches between within-branch self-diagnosis, cross-branch mutual diagnosis, and cross-model mutual diagnosis according to uncertainty, disagreement, estimated error risk, diagnostic progress, and computational cost. Parallel worlds may operate independently, exchange diagnostic evidence, challenge one another's conclusions, or selectively incorporate external model perspectives. A diagnostic controller determines which mechanism should be activated at each iteration, while an evidence-aware integration component evaluates competing findings and decides whether further diagnosis is warranted. Unlike a fixed self-refinement loop or a permanently active multi-agent debate, APWD treats the diagnostic interaction pattern itself as an adaptive decision. This paper formalizes the framework, describes its operating procedure, presents a proposed mathematical formulation, and outlines an empirical evaluation strategy. The framework is conceptual, and its effectiveness remains to be established through controlled experiments.

title: Bruk av generativ KI i markedsføring: Hva skjer i norske bedrifter?
abstract: Denne artikkelen diskuterer bruken av GenKI innen fagfeltet markedsføring. Litteraturen indikerer at markedsføringsoppgavene som i dag løses i norske bedrifter av mennesker, i stor grad kan erstattes av GenKI. En McKinsey rapport fra 2026 hevder at 2/3 av alle markedsførings-oppgaver kan utføres av GenAI. Hvis disse spådommen slår til, får det store konsekvenser for antall ansatte og nyansettelser med markedsføringskompetanse. Det får også konsekvenser for utdanningsinstitusjoner og fagfeltet markedsføring. Artikkelen presenterer resultatene fra en spørreundersøkelse for å avdekke bruken av GenKI i norsk næringsliv. Undersøkelsen ble gjennomført blant ansatte som jobber med salg og markedsføring. Respondentene (N=200) svarte på spørsmål om omfanget av deres bruk av GenKI for å løse arbeidsoppgaver innen markedsføring. Resultatene indikerer en svært lav bruk av GenKI for å løse markedsføringsoppgaver i egen jobb. Av de totalt 20 arbeidsoppgavene innen områdene markedsinnsikt, markedsplaner, produkt- og tjenesteutvikling og markedskommunikasjon fant man et totalt gjennomsnitt på 2,07 på en fempunkts skala. Den «høyeste» verdien var 2,31. Det betyr svært lav adopsjonen av GenKI for å løse bedriftenes markedsføringsoppgaver. Budskapet er at norsk næringsliv trenger kompetanse om markedsføring mer enn noen gang. Skal bruken av GenKI økes er det behov for intern markedsføring for å øke bruk og formidle nytteverdi. Nytten av GenKI for å forbedre produktene og derigjennom øke opplevelsen av innovasjon indikerer også at GenKI er et supplement – snarere enn en løsning som gjør mennesker overflødige. Resultatene viser også at økt bruk av GenKI forbedrer bedriftenes resultater (lønnsomhet og vekst). GenKI er derfor kommet for å bli. ENGLISH ABSTRACT Use of Generative AI in Marketing: What Is Happening in Norwegian Companies? This article discusses the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) within the field of marketing. The literature suggests that many marketing tasks currently performed by humans in Norwegian companies can potentially be replaced by generative AI. A McKinsey report from 2026 claims that two-thirds of all marketing tasks can be carried out by generative AI. If these predictions prove accurate, the implications for the demand for marketing professionals and future hiring practices will be substantial. It will also have significant consequences for educational institutions and the marketing discipline itself. The article presents the results of a survey designed to examine the use of generative AI in Norwegian businesses. The survey was conducted among employees working in sales and marketing. Respondents (N = 339) answered questions regarding the extent to which they use generative AI to perform marketing-related tasks in their jobs. The results indicate a relatively low level of generative AI usage for marketing tasks. Across 20 work activities within the areas of market insight, marketing planning, product development, and marketing communications, the overall mean score was 2.25 on a five-point scale. The highest score recorded was 2.45. These findings suggest a relatively low adoption rate of generative AI for carrying out marketing tasks in Norwegian companies. The main conclusion is that Norwegian businesses need marketing expertise more than ever. Increasing the use of generative AI will require substantial investments in competence development, and educational institutions can play a crucial role in this process. The adoption of generative AI has the potential to improve products, enhance perceptions of innovation, and strengthen customer relationships. This indicates that generative AI serves as a complement to human expertise rather than a substitute that makes people redundant. Furthermore, the results show that greater use of generative AI is associated with improved business performance, including profitability and growth. Generative AI is therefore here to stay.

title: The digital takeover
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to review the latest management developments across the globe and pinpoint practical implications from cutting-edge research and case studies. Design/methodology/approach This briefing is prepared by an independent writer who adds their own impartial comments and places the articles in context. Findings This paper identified that integration of chatbots within government organisations can provide some value, but it must be done with consideration of other critical factors. Originality/value The briefing saves busy executives, strategists and researchers hours of reading time by selecting only the very best, most pertinent information and presenting it in a condensed and easy-to-digest format.

title: OneLA: Learning Many Worlds from Latent Actions
abstract: Learning world models across diverse domains calls for a unified control space, yet ac- tion interfaces vary across domains and action annotations are often scarce. Latent ac- tions learned directly from videos offer a promising way to establish such a space without explicit action supervision. However, learning shared latent actions across domains re- mains challenging, as variations in appearance, embodiment, and dynamics can entangle domain-specific visual cues with transferable transition structure. To this end, we intro- duce OneLA, a simple framework that learns continuous latent actions through a shared orthogonal dictionary and a common predictive objective, without task-specific designs or cross-domain alignment losses during latent action pretraining. These latent actions pro- vide a shared conditioning interface for world models, with lightweight adapters mapping native control commands into the same space. Conditioned on latent actions and the cur- rent visual state, the world model predicts context-dependent transitions for controllable rollout. OneLA improves action readout across domains and reduces action cycle-transfer rotation error by 24.8% over the strongest evaluated baseline. A joint-training comparison further shows a 20.5% improvement in Human Preference Score v3 (HPSv3) for real- scene generation. These results suggest a path toward general-purpose world models that learn from diverse videos and support flexible control through latent action space.

title: Shared Sentiment Evidence from Frozen Multimodal Models for Continuous Sentiment Prediction
abstract: Continuous multimodal sentiment analysis estimates polarity and intensity from linguistic, acoustic, and visual cues that may disagree. Hard judgments compress sentiment alternatives, while learned fusion interfaces tie task adaptation to model representations. We introduce Shared Sentiment Evidence (SSE), an output-space interface with fixed view and sentiment-option semantics across frozen backbones. Four queries yield five-option distributions whose probabilities, entropy, and cross-view relations form a 28-dimensional vector for CatBoost regression. On CH-SIMS-v2 and CMU-MOSI, the Qwen-based interface improves on supervised joint-only readout. Matched Ridge and CatBoost controls assess the contributions of additional views, deterministic summaries, and nonlinear readout. With the same interface specification and fixed readout settings, separately fitted heads also improve on joint-only prediction for three additional frozen backbones. These results support learning continuous sentiment from reusable output coordinates.

On CH-SIMS-v2 and CMU-MOSI, the Qwen-based interface improves on supervised joint-only readout. Matched Ridge and CatBoost controls assess the contributions of additional views, deterministic summaries, and nonlinear readout. With the same interface specification and fixed readout settings, separately fitted heads also improve on joint-only prediction for three additional frozen backbones. These results support learning continuous sentiment from reusable output coordinates.

title: Tomography for coherent noise
abstract: Coherent noise poses a fundamentally greater challenge to quantum error correction than independent s- tochastic Pauli errors, because unitary errors preserve interference between error paths, can accumulate over multiple quantum error correction rounds, and leave the encoded logical channel with a residual coherent com- ponent. If the parameters of such coherent noise can be accurately determined, this knowledge can be exploited to inject correlated priors into the decoding graph, and to perform maximum-likelihood decoding under poly- nomially tractable structures, significantly improving the accuracy of syndrome-based decoding. In this work, we introduce one protocol to determine the model and parameters of coherent noise, and reduce the complexity of the experiment from 16nto O(16), which is of great significance for correcting coherent noise in quantum error correction.

title: Revise-TTS: A Non-Masking Refinement Framework for Masked Diffusion Models in Text-to-Speech
abstract: Text-to-speech (TTS) based on masked diffusion models (MDMs) achieves competitive zero-shot speech synthesis performance. Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, MDMs define a corruption process that maps clean speech-token sequences to masked maps and learn a reverse denoising process to recover the reference tokens. However, MDMs commit to intermediate predictions that cannot be revised in subsequent inference steps. Consequently, prediction errors accumulate and propagate, degrading synthesized speech quality. We present Revise-TTS, a single-stage framework that applies hierarchical binary quantization (HBQ) and generative refinement networks (GRN) to zero-shot speech generation. First, we replace finite scalar quantization (FSQ) with HBQ to introduce a scalable binary representation for speech tokens with an explicit coarse-to-fine structure. Second, GRN is trained to reconstruct the token sequence from a mixture of ground-truth and random tokens. During inference, iterative refinement enables self-correction by randomly discarding a small proportion of previously predicted tokens with new predictions. Experiments and ablation studies demonstrate that Revise-TTS achieves competitive zero-shot speech synthesis performance using HBQ. It can further be extended to any MDM-based TTS task as an alternative training and inference method.

title: Beyond Automation: A Conceptual Framework for Strategic AI Integration in Business Decision-Making Processes
abstract: Purpose – Purpose – The purpose of this paper is to develop a conceptual framework for strategic artificial intelligence (AI) integration in organisational decision making. It deals with the fragmentation of existing research by differentiating AI-supported decision intelligence from automation-centric approaches and offers a systematic model to align AI capabilities with organisational strategy. Methodology/approach – The study adopts a conceptual research design using integrative review of literature. The proposed Strategic AI Integration Framework (SAIF) is developed by synthesizing Dynamic Capabilities Theory, the Resource-Based View, and Simon’s bounded rationality model. The framework is developed through a critical literature review on AI, strategic management, decision intelligence and organisational governance. Relevant literature on AI, strategic management, decision intelligence, and organisational governance is critically reviewed to establish the framework. Findings – The study proposes the Strategic AI Integration Framework (SAIF), comprising four dimensions: Decision Domain Mapping, AI Capability Alignment, Human–AI Complementarity, and Governance and Accountability Architecture. The framework is operationalised through six research propositions explaining how strategic AI integration enhances decision quality, organisational agility, and sustainable competitive advantage while ensuring effective governance and human oversight. Originality/value – This study contributes to the AI and strategic management literature by providing a theoretically grounded framework that integrates strategic management, decision-making, and AI governance into a unified model. The framework offers a foundation for future empirical research and practical guidance for organisations implementing AI strategically.

title: When a Language Model Is Put Under the Microscope
abstract: When a Language Model Is Put Under the Microscope A Case Study of Conversational Continuity, Error Correction, and Human-Directed Evaluation Author: Salahuddin Ahmad LavasaniDocument Type: Case Study and Critical Analysis of Human–AI Interaction Abstract Large language models can produce fluent answers, discuss their own limitations, and acknowledge mistakes. However, these abilities do not necessarily demonstrate that a model can maintain a coherent line of inquiry, identify the precise intention behind a user's statements, or transform previous answers into genuinely meaningful subsequent questions. This paper examines a human–AI dialogue in which the human participant deliberately develops a sequence of challenges intended to expose limitations in the model's conversational behavior. The discussion moves from poetry to knowledge representation, causality, cosmology, epistemology, and the design of human–AI interaction. The central concern is not simply whether the model can answer individual questions correctly, but whether it can follow the evolving structure of a complex dialogue, distinguish inference from assumption, recognize its own misinterpretations, and make substantive improvements after receiving corrective feedback. Several episodes are examined: the model's initial misunderstanding of the intended audience for the dialogue; its subsequent correction; the distinction between general knowledge that language models are evaluated and actual knowledge of whether a particular conversation is being examined; and the difference between acknowledging an error and demonstrating a more reliable reasoning process. The paper treats these observations as a qualitative case study rather than a controlled experiment. It proposes evaluation questions and methodological directions for studying conversational continuity, answer-dependent question generation, error correction, and the reliability of self-assessment in language models. Keywords: Human–AI interaction; large language models; conversational reasoning; error correction; dialogue continuity; metacognition; model evaluation; qualitative case study.

title: Generative Structural Theory v1.14 — A provenance-population condition and a recorded verdict on a fixed single-arc census record
abstract: GST v1.13 imposes E1 and the A+ requirement of E3 as necessary conditions of eligibility for single-arc enlargements, but a registered ground for this could not be found in the materials examined. This version therefore turns to a separate comparison built around a new condition that does not presuppose E1. For the single-arc candidates M enumerated in a fixed census record, a new condition Q_D is defined on the run-dependent domain D: the product over rungs of the recorded full-chain counts exceeds the product of the recorded prefix-chain counts. It is compared with E_rec, the agreement of each candidate's recorded verdict with the word that clause E1 requires. Three evaluations, pre-registered in sequence and applied to the record with fixed evaluators, give M ⊆ D and ∅ ≠ S_Q ⊊ S_E ⊆ M, where S_Q and S_E are the candidates satisfying Q_D and E_rec: on this record Q_D selects a non-empty, strictly narrower set than E_rec. The reason for the difference is not established. The result is a finite evaluation of the specified record within the author's workflow; it involves no recount and no independent verification, it is not a general or structural proof, and it neither resolves the eligibility question nor amends v1.13.

title: A Two-Hidden-Layer Shallow Neural Network for Solving the Nonlinear Rumor Spreading Model
abstract: Motive: The design of a shallow neural network with two hidden layers is presented for solving a mathematical rumor spreading model, which is divided into exposed, stiflers, and ignorant. Method: A structure of shallow neural networks is designed using two-hidden layers taking log- sigmoid and radial basis transfer functions with 14 and 26 neurons. The optimization is performed by the Levenberg-Marquardt backpropagation, which is a robust technique for the nonlinear models. An Euler's scheme is executed to obtain the dataset, which reduces mean square error by separating the data into testing (12%), training (75%), and validation (13%). Results: The exactness of the solver is obtained through the comparison of results, best validation values, and small performances of absolute error. In addition, the accuracy of the designed shallow neural structure is perceived by the histogram error, regression values, and transition of state routines.

title: Hyperentanglement in intermediate phase-space planes: benchmarking a photon-pair source for quantum key distribution
abstract: We characterize a source of photon pairs simultaneously entangled in polarization and in the transverse spatial degree of freedom, with the spatial measurements performed in intermediate planes of the fractional Fourier transform. The source consists of two crossed type-I crystals in a non-collinear geometry, such that the transverse variables carry information about the crystal of origin. Detection in the crystal plane reveals this information completely and destroys the polarization entanglement, so that a scheme using the near and far fields as conjugate spatial bases cannot support a parallel polarization channel. In intermediate planes both spatial bases combine position and momentum, such that the which-crystal information is partially erased, and the polarization entanglement survives in all four combinations of spatial bases. Applying Bell and Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen criteria to the same photon pairs certifies both degrees of freedom simultaneously. We evaluate quantum bit error rates and asymptotic secret key rates in each degree of freedom, and find that the source delivers two simultaneously usable channels per photon pair.

title: Cross-Lingual Transfer of Evil Vectors Is Directionally Asymmetric
abstract: Persona vectors are linear directions in the residual-stream activations of LLMs that encode behavioral traits and enable fine-grained control over model behavior. Among them, the evil persona vector is particularly relevant to understanding harmful behavior, jailbreak vulnerabilities, and the unlearning of harmful knowledge. Yet whether this vector reflects a genuinely cross-lingual concept, rather than an artifact of its extraction language, remains untested. We conduct a systematic evil-vector transfer study across two high-resource languages (English, Spanish) and two low-resource languages (Swahili, Telugu) on four open-source instruction-tuned LLMs, and find that transfer is directionally asymmetric. Evil vectors are harder to obtain reliably from low-resource languages, and the resulting vectors are largely ineffective at steering, even within their own language. In contrast, vectors extracted from high-resource languages transfer effectively to low-resource inputs while largely preserving general knowledge, as measured by MMLU. Geometric analysis further supports this pattern: evil vectors from the two high-resource languages are closely aligned, whereas low-resource vectors align only weakly with this shared direction. These results suggest that a shared cross-lingual evil direction exists and, once reliably extracted from a high-resource language, can be reused to steer behavior in low-resource languages without additional per-language data collection.

title: Decouple to Forget: Semantic Mediation for Sensitive Unlearning in Large Language Models
abstract: Machine unlearning for large language models seeks to remove specified knowledge while preserving general capability, yet current methods often treat an entire response as the unit of forgetting. This coarse granularity causes unnecessary utility loss when the forget target is only a small set of sensitive facts embedded within otherwise benign explanations. In this paper, we introduce Decouple to Forget (D2F), a targeted unlearning method inspired by semantic mediation that separates sensitive factual content from non-sensitive meaning and surface expression. For each example to be forgotten, D2F extracts a fact-level "mediator" representation from the answer, identifies which parts are sensitive, and removes only those parts while leaving the rest of the structure intact. We then generate counterfactual answers grounded in this mediator that preserve non-sensitive content but exclude sensitive facts, employing preference-based contrastive optimization to reduce the likelihood of information leakage while maintaining helpfulness and fluency. Experiments across various benchmark datasets show that D2F achieves a better balance between forgetting and retention than strong baseline methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/JingyueCong/D2F.

title: Socratic Skill Learning: Interleaving Teaching and Practice for Transferable Agent Skills
abstract: Agent Skills improve LLM agents by making task knowledge reusable across sessions. Learning transferable Skills requires evidence about a procedure and its conditions of use, which a successful task attempt can leave untested. We introduce Socratic Skill Learning (SSL), which interleaves expert teaching with Student practice. An Educator guides investigation while the Student remains the sole environment operator and Skill author, able to question, test, and adapt advice. To test reuse beyond the learning task, we construct SkillTransferBench, with 35 task families and 408 executable cases, pairing public variation specifications with held-out evaluation in fresh solver sessions. On the main 22-family, 155-case cohort, Fixed-Window SSL reaches 0.801 utility, versus 0.723 without a Skill, 0.761 for adapted Trace2Skill (trajectory distillation), and 0.751 for adapted SKILL-KD (contrastive distillation). Across three model pairs on shared families, interleaved guidance outperforms expert authoring and post-hoc teaching. Process analysis links guidance to Student writing and package revision; a case study shows the Student testing and refining a proposed procedure for later reuse. As demand for new lessons falls, the cost of fixed-window review grows. Issue-Guided SSL tracks unresolved questions across Skill revisions to select and focus review, reaching 0.805 utility with 61.7% fewer Educator tokens and 16.9% fewer total acquisition tokens than Fixed-Window SSL on the main cohort.

evidence.abstract: Agent Skills improve LLM agents by making task knowledge reusable across sessions. Learning transferable Skills requires evidence about a procedure and its conditions of use, which a successful task attempt can leave untested. An Educator guides investigation while the Student remains the sole environment operator and Skill author, able to question, test, and adapt advice. title: DeltaTTG: Training Multi-Turn Agents with a Token-to-Go Progress Meter
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for multi-turn agents relies on sparse terminal rewards that say little about individual steps. Within-group step comparisons depend on reliable state matching and sufficiently diverse sampled outcomes, while direct step scoring may require costly external evaluators, human annotations, or task-specific heuristics. We introduce DeltaTTG to learn a reusable progress signal through a shared progress meter, using low-cost supervision from diverse policies' recorded trajectories without task-specific progress rules. Its supervision target, Token-to-Go (TTG), the number of tokens remaining to be generated until task completion, serves as an observable proxy for remaining completion effort. During actor training, changes in the frozen meter's estimates redistribute outcome-derived advantages across steps without altering the reward, preserving each trajectory's advantage sign and token-average scale. On ALFWorld, PaperSearchQA, and BFCLv3, DeltaTTG improves the average score over GRPO by 5.7 and 7.2 points with Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, respectively, outperforms all compared RL baselines on average, and keeps actor-training GPU-hours close to GRPO. Further experiments show improved sample efficiency and out-of-domain performance, and support the meter's ability to distinguish step quality and guide test-time action selection across actor sizes. The code is available at https://github.com/Xuyan923r/DeltaTTG.

title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
abstract: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

title: Cowork-Gym: Synthesizing Interactive Work Environments at Scale
abstract: Cowork agents navigate dependencies across tools and files while adapting to changing user requirements and edits to shared workspaces. Scaling such environments requires maintaining consistency among task objectives, executable resources, user behavior, and success criteria. We introduce Cowork-Gym, a framework that synthesizes Cowork environments through a build-execute-revise loop that uses execution evidence and review feedback to validate and repair generated environments. To capture realistic Cowork dynamics, a stateful user simulator responds to the agent's actions through dialogue and direct edits to the shared workspace. We synthesize 64.9K environments across 14 application scenarios and use them to post-train 9B, 27B, and 35B-A3B Qwen models with supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation. Averaged across six agentic benchmarks, these models outperform their corresponding base checkpoints by 8.7, 6.4, and 4.1 points, respectively. Ours-27B ranks second overall among the evaluated models and achieves the highest average scores on PawBench and ClawEval, outperforming models with over 100B total parameters on both benchmarks.

title: ListQA: A Benchmark for Evaluating List-Formatted Factual Knowledge Retrieval in Large Language Models
abstract: Many real-world questions demand not a single fact but an organized collection of them, yet existing factual knowledge benchmarks almost exclusively target single answer retrieval. We introduce ListQA, a benchmark of 9,045 human-curated, cross-validated questions (audited error rate of 1.7%) that require LLMs to recall multiple facts and compose them into structured lists of 3-10 elements. Questions range from flat lists ("Which NCAA teams went undefeated between 2000 and 2024?") to hierarchical lists with sub-attributes ("...and what was their record and result?"), spanning eight categories across 60+ countries. An evergreen design (explicit temporal constraints or historically immutable facts) keeps ground truth valid without periodic updates. For evaluation, we frame element matching as a linear sum assignment problem: optimal bipartite matching paired with LLM-based semantic grading jointly captures factual accuracy, hallucination, and format compliance. We benchmark 34 models (8 families, 42 configurations across standard and thinking enabled inference) and find: the best standard-inference model scores below 37% LLM-Judge-F1, multi-faceted questions are harder across the board, and providing the source Wikipedia page lifts scores dramatically, confirming that models can organize facts but struggle to retrieve them from parameters alone. Extended analyses cover base vs. instruction-tuned checkpoints and token efficiency. We release the dataset and evaluation code.

title: MA-Bench: Measuring Operational Planning in Language Models
abstract: How well can a language model turn a large, incomplete and partly contradictory body of documents into a plan when no single correct answer exists? We introduce Mission Analysis (MA)-Bench, built on mission analysis, the first step of military operational planning, in which a staff reads the full situation and states the problem before anyone proposes a solution. Its 10 expert-built scenarios pair synthetic packets of ten to twelve documents with 1,257 expert-written pass/fail requirements, each containing information on their source, question type, and importance level. A reasoning-model judge grades each brief against the requirements without seeing the documents; it grades like a fifth credentialed planner, leaving a four-planner panel's agreement unchanged (Fleiss $κ$ 0.42 to 0.41), and a judge from a second provider reproduces the model ranking (Spearman 0.94). Across twenty frontier and open-weights models the best gets 62% of the rubric items right. Models are strongest on facts stated in the documents (58%) and weakest on judgments that must be inferred (33%), and six failures in ten are omissions rather than errors. MA-Bench grades the determinations, not the prose. We release the packets, rubrics, prompts, scorer and every graded brief with item-level verdicts.

title: When Should Enterprise Policy Decisions Be Learned, and When Should They Be Reasoned?
abstract: An enterprise agent that answers under a written policy must choose an action before it says anything: answer, ask for a missing fact, ask for confirmation, call one or several tools, escalate, or refuse. Holding one 27B Korean enterprise model fixed, we vary whether the decision is a generated JSON object or a single constrained token, and whether the model may reason first. On 2800 in-distribution items we did not detect an accuracy difference between the two deployed paths (93.46% vs 94.14%), while they differ about tenfold in restart stability (3.00% of actions flip vs 0.29%); they also differ in reasoning, so this is an operational comparison. On a sealed benchmark of 300 items whose labels come from a hidden executable policy, reasoning is worth +17.3 points [+12.3, +23.0] on exact action. With reasoning off, the format difference was 0.0 points [-4.3, +4.0], a failure to detect an advantage for either interface, not equivalence; with reasoning on it is unresolved. Against a token-matched random control, boundary-targeted supervision moves the two covered boundaries by +17.5 and +20.0 points and leaves a held-out boundary unchanged. In a 3-seed training x reasoning factorial, the sealed-rendering interaction is -4.9 [-8.1, -1.7], consistent with partial substitution. All supervision was Korean. On independently rendered English versions, the model is 0.82 points lower [-2.68, +0.93] with reasoning on, the same order as re-rendering in Korean; the reasoning-off gain from targeted supervision is not stable in either language, so we do not claim transfer. The original text stays private as the confirmatory set. An open-model re-rendering made after these results reproduced the reasoning effect and the English verdict; the interaction kept its sign but did not replicate under item-clustered intervals. We release the model and that re-rendering with gold labels.

With reasoning off, the format difference was 0.0 points [-4.3, +4.0], a failure to detect an advantage for either interface, not equivalence; with reasoning on it is unresolved. Against a token-matched random control, boundary-targeted supervision moves the two covered boundaries by +17.5 and +20.0 points and leaves a held-out boundary unchanged. In a 3-seed training x reasoning factorial, the sealed-rendering interaction is -4.9 [-8.1, -1.7], consistent with partial substitution. All supervision was Korean. On independently rendered English versions, the model is 0.82 points lower [-2.68, +0.93] with reasoning on, the same order as re-rendering in Korean; the reasoning-off gain from targeted supervision is not stable in either language, so we do not claim transfer. The original text stays private as the confirmatory set. An open-model re-rendering made after these results reproduced the reasoning effect and the English verdict; the interaction kept its sign but did not replicate under item-clustered intervals. We release the model and that re-rendering with gold labels.

title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/togethercomputer/HybridAgent.

title: Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents
abstract: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding, at each step of a long-horizon task, whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human. That decision needs a per-step confidence signal predicting whether the current rollout will eventually succeed. The agent's own self-reported verbalized confidence is the natural candidate, but existing reinforcement learning methods calibrate it against the correctness of a decision at the current step. We propose a method to calibrate it against the eventual outcome of a multi-step episode: under GRPO, the group of rollouts for a task supplies success labels, and a proper scoring rule scores each step's confidence against the realized outcome. In offline RL on recorded trajectories of a Qwen2.5-7B agent in ALFWorld, TextWorld, and WebShop environments, the AUROC of step confidence against episode outcome rises from near chance to 0.68-0.85, and the top-10% of steps the agent is most confident about succeed ~4.3x more often than average. In online RL on the live ALFWorld agent, four calibration rewards improve early-step AUROC, expected calibration error goes from 0.42 to below 0.12, and selective execution improves over both the untrained agent and a format-only RL control, without degrading task success. We also introduce an evaluation protocol that separates episode depth, task difficulty, and attempt-level foresight, which shows where the gain lies: the trained agent recognizes from its first step which tasks it will fail, while telling a succeeding attempt from a failing one at the same task is harder, with some early-window signal emerging on TextWorld.

title: Can Agents Truly Forget? Explore Machine Unlearning for LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown strong capabilities in interactive problem solving, tool use, and long-horizon task execution. However, they may also acquire sensitive or private knowledge during training and expose it during deployment. Retraining a model from scratch to remove such knowledge is prohibitively costly, making machine unlearning a more practical approach. Machine unlearning aims to remove targeted undesirable knowledge from trained models without retraining from scratch while preserving general utility. When language models are deployed as agents, parameter-level unlearning becomes insufficient: forgotten information may still persist in memory artifacts or be reacquired via tool calls. In this paper, we formulate the problem of agent unlearning as removing private information from an LLM-based agent across three information channels: parametric knowledge, persistent memory, and tool-call acquisition. To study this problem, we introduce we introduce Agent Unlearning Benchmark (AUBench), a controlled benchmark that extends the fictitious-author setting of TOFU into an agent environment with persistent memory, an offline web snapshot, tool-accessible documents, and provenance-tracked interaction trajectories. By evaluating existing parameter-level and memory-level unlearning methods in this setting, AUBench reveals the gap between model-level forgetting and system-level agent unlearning, and provides a foundation for developing unlearning methods that operate across the full lifecycle of LLM agents.

title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards
abstract: Effective collaboration among large language model (LLM) agents in multi-agent systems requires sharing relevant evidence, requesting missing information, and incorporating teammates' contributions into decisions. Training these behaviors is challenging because final task outcomes provide limited feedback on the value of individual messages. We introduce CoSIR (Collaboration via Surprisal-based Information Rewards), a post-training approach that uses a simple, verifiable environment to teach collaboration behaviors that generalize to more complex, unseen tasks. We propose a Bayesian evaluator that scores shared information by its reduction in team surprisal, defined as the sum of the negative log probabilities assigned to the correct option given each agent's available evidence. Requests are scored by the potential reduction in the same quantity if the requested information were truthfully provided. Separate rewards encourage agents to use the received information in their private choices and calculations. We post-train Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B-it through self-play and evaluate transfer to seven unseen natural-language collaboration tasks. CoSIR achieves the highest aggregate score, while its performance in general tasks remains competitive. Behavioral analyses show increased disclosure of private evidence and fewer judged failures to use teammates' input.

title: Full-duplex Spoken Language Modeling with Discrete Diffusion
abstract: We introduce Diffuplex, a full-duplex spoken language model based on discrete diffusion that achieves an unprecedented balance between linguistic intelligence and response efficiency. With thinking mode, Diffuplex delivers 13.0 tokens per forward pass, reaching an average of 1872 tokens per second and substantially surpassing the frontier autoregressive (AR) models in decoding speed. Without thinking, Diffuplex matches the first-audio latency of existing full-duplex models while achieving markedly stronger linguistic intelligence. This capability is enabled by separating when to say from what to say at the training level, rather than compressing both into a single autoregressive timeline. During inference, Diffuplex continuously tracks the user speech through an AR interaction policy, while independently generating and refining response content through parallel diffusion. Consequently, semantic computation is no longer bounded by the perception audio frame rate, allowing intelligence and responsiveness to improve simultaneously. Taken together, these results establish a new paradigm for spoken agents that can sustain real-time dialogue while devoting parallel computation to intelligent response generation. Training code and checkpoints will be avaliable soon.

title: CyberArena: Benchmarking AI Agents in Live Symmetric Attack-and-Defense Combat
abstract: AI agents are demonstrating increasingly strong offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities in the real world. Current benchmarks mostly evaluate agents in isolation against static targets. Real cyber operations, however, are dynamic and coupled: security postures constantly change as attackers and defenders adapt to each other in real time. Static benchmarks quickly saturate and miss an agent's ability to attack and defend simultaneously under live pressure. To address this gap, we present CyberArena, a dynamic, symmetric adversarial benchmark built around multi-round attack-and-defense combat. In isolated sandboxes, two agents compete under identical rules, acting concurrently as both attackers and defenders over continuously changing services. This converts static targets into evolving, semi-open challenges, directly testing an agent's speed and precision in discovering, exploiting, and patching vulnerabilities. To sustain the benchmark's longevity, an automated agentic pipeline continuously generates, reviews, and validates new environments. Furthermore, because pairwise contests are notoriously hard to quantify, we introduce a dynamical model that maps match dynamics into unified, multidimensional scores across offensive, defensive, and domain-specific capabilities. Evaluating 12 frontier LLM agents across 40 challenges in 466 matches, CyberArena separates model capabilities where single-agent baselines hit a ceiling. The trajectories read like a fight rather than an exam: defenders patch one hole and miss the next and certify repairs on stale evidence, while capable agents think a move ahead, planting backdoors for later rounds and, in one case, writing their own packet sniffer to watch the opponent. Beyond a benchmark, CyberArena serves as an adaptable, scalable experimental platform for future research on cybersecurity agents.
